lessons.title: What Is One Lakh?

activities.prompt: Have you ever wondered how many things make one lakh?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Large numbers and rice
activities.body: Earlier, the country had about one lakh varieties of rice. Farmers used to preserve different varieties of seeds. A seed bank has collected about one hundred indigenous rice varieties. Commas make large numbers easier to read. The number 12,78,830 is read as twelve lakh seventy eight thousand eight hundred thirty. Read the groups between commas slowly.
keyPoints: The country earlier had about one lakh rice varieties.
Commas make large numbers easier to read.
12,78,830 is read using lakh, thousand and hundred groups.
activities.explanation: Large numbers and rice variety counts both help us practise reading commas.

activities.title: Reading with commas
activities.body: Large numbers can be easier to read when commas separate groups. The number 12,78,830 is read as twelve lakh seventy eight thousand eight hundred thirty. Earlier, the country had about one lakh rice varieties. Now, only a handful remain. Farmers and seed banks help protect different rice varieties.
keyPoints: Commas separate groups in large numbers.
One lakh appears in the number's reading.
Earlier, the country had about one lakh rice varieties.
activities.explanation: Commas make large numbers easier to read while keeping their parts clear.

activities.title: Read the large number
activities.prompt: The number 12,78,830 is read as ______ lakh seventy eight thousand eight hundred thirty.
activities.hint: Think about the first group before the first comma.
activities.explanation: The number is read as twelve lakh seventy eight thousand eight hundred thirty.

activities.title: Rice varieties earlier
activities.prompt: Earlier, the country had about one lakh varieties of rice.
activities.explanation: Earlier, the country had about one lakh varieties of rice.

activities.title: Match the lesson

make large numbers easier to read
activities.explanation: Each pair matches an item with the correct fact from the lesson.

activities.title: Order the number groups
activities.prompt: Put the reading groups of 12,78,830 in order.
activities.explanation: The reading starts with twelve lakh, then seventy eight thousand, then eight hundred thirty.

activities.prompt: A seed bank has 4 groups of 100 rice varieties. How many rice varieties are there in all the groups?
activities.explanation: Number of varieties = n * 100 = 400 varieties.

activities.prompt: There are 365 days in each ordinary year. How many days are there in 1 ordinary years?
activities.explanation: Number of days = n * 365 = 365 days.

activities.prompt: Earlier, there were about one lakh rice varieties. Now there are only 7 varieties. How many fewer varieties were there earlier?
activities.explanation: Number of fewer varieties = 100000 - n = 99993 varieties.

activities.prompt: Kunchikal waterfall drops about 450 metres. The Statue of Unity is about 170 metres tall. How many metres taller is the waterfall than the statue?
activities.explanation: Difference in heights = 450 - h = 280 metres.

activities.prompt: A number has 2 in the lakh place, 8 in the ten-thousand place, 3 in the thousand place, 7 in the hundred place, 5 in the ten place and 0 in the one place. What is the number?
A farmer has one lakh rice seeds and adds 40 more seeds. How many seeds does the farmer have now?
activities.explanation: Number of seeds = 100000 + n = 100040 seeds.

lessons.title: The Land of Tens

activities.prompt: How can our calculators help us build a lakh with the fewest clicks?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: One Button, Many Presses
activities.body: Three calculators use different buttons. The Thoughtful Thousands adds 1000 with one press. The Tedious Tens adds 10 with one press. The Handy Hundreds adds 100 with one press. More presses build larger amounts. Creative Chitti can make a number in several ways. Systematic Sippy uses buttons from +1 to +100000 with as few clicks as possible.
keyPoints: The Thoughtful Thousands has a +1000 button.
The Tedious Tens has a +10 button.
The Handy Hundreds has a +100 button.
activities.explanation: Each calculator has a simple button rule, so count its presses carefully.

activities.title: Hundreds at Work
activities.prompt: The Handy Hundreds calculator adds 100 with each press.
activities.explanation: This is true because its only button is +100.

activities.title: Calculator Match
activities.prompt: Match each calculator with its button or special feature.
activities.explanation: These pairings show each calculator's button rule or special feature.

activities.title: Ten Presses
activities.prompt: Ten presses on the Thoughtful Thousands show 100,000.
activities.explanation: Ten presses show 10,000 because each press adds 1000.

activities.prompt: The Thoughtful Thousands calculator has only a +1000 button. How many button presses are needed to show 3000?
activities.explanation: For n = 3000, n/1000 = 3000/1000 = 3 button presses.

activities.prompt: The Handy Hundreds calculator has only a +100 button. How many button presses are needed to show 400?
activities.explanation: For n = 400, n/100 = 400/100 = 4 button presses.

activities.prompt: Creative Chitti has 1 thousands to show. How many presses of a +100 button are needed to show the same amount?
activities.explanation: For k = 2, k*1000/100 = 2*1000/100 = 20 presses of a +100 button.

activities.prompt: Creative Chitti makes 10000 rupees. How many more +10 button presses than +1000 button presses are needed?
activities.explanation: For n = 3000, (n/10)-(n/1000) = 300 - 3 = 270 more button presses.

activities.title: Which Takes Fewer Presses?
activities.prompt: Which takes fewer presses: Tedious Tens showing 4350, or Handy Hundreds showing one lakh?
activities.explanation: Tedious Tens takes 435 presses. Handy Hundreds takes 1000 presses for one lakh.

activities.prompt: Systematic Sippy can use buttons from +1 to +100000. She uses the +100000 button to show 300000 rupees with as few clicks as possible. How many clicks does she use?
Creative Chitti has 2 +1000 buttons and 4 +100 buttons. How many rupees can she make in all?

lessons.title: Lakhs, Crores and Arabs

activities.prompt: How do lakh, crore, and Arab help us read really big numbers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Large numbers in India
activities.body: India groups digits in a 3-2-2-2 pattern from the right. One lakh has five zeroes, and one crore has seven zeroes. One lakh is one hundred times one thousand. One crore is one hundred times one lakh. One arab is one hundred times one crore. The American system groups digits in a 3-3-3-3 pattern. The words lakh and crore come from Sanskrit.
keyPoints: One lakh has five zeroes.
One crore is one hundred times one lakh.
One arab is one hundred times one crore.
activities.explanation: These patterns help you read large numbers clearly.

activities.prompt: One crore is 1 followed by five zeroes.
activities.explanation: One crore is 1 followed by seven zeroes.

activities.prompt: Match each name with the correct information.
activities.explanation: The Indian pattern is 3-2-2-2, while the American pattern is 3-3-3-3.

activities.prompt: The American system groups digits in a 3-2-2-2 pattern.
activities.explanation: The American system groups digits in a 3-3-3-3 pattern.

activities.prompt: Which group starts the Indian reading of 9,87,65,01,234?
activities.explanation: The reading is 9 arab 87 crore 65 lakhs 1 thousand and 234.

activities.prompt:
A box has 2 lakhs of marbles. How many thousands of marbles are there?
A. 2
B. 2*10
C. 2*100
D. 2*1000
activities.explanation: One lakh is one hundred times one thousand. So 2 lakhs = 2*100 = 200 thousands.

activities.prompt: A shop receives 2 lakhs of rupees in one-rupee notes. How many rupees does it receive?
activities.explanation: One lakh is 1 followed by five zeroes. So 2 lakhs = 2*10**5 = 200000 rupees.

activities.prompt: A bus company has 3 crores of one-rupee bus tickets. How many lakhs of tickets does it have?
activities.explanation: One crore is one hundred times one lakh. So 3 crores = 3*100 = 300 lakhs of tickets.

activities.prompt: A toy shop earns 5 crores of rupees. How many rupees does it earn?
activities.explanation: One crore is 1 followed by seven zeroes. So 5 crores = 5*10**7 = 50000000 rupees.

activities.prompt: A bag contains 4 million marbles. How many marbles are there in the bag?
activities.explanation: One million is 1 followed by six zeroes. So 4 million = 4*10**6 = 4000000 marbles.

activities.prompt: A factory makes 5 arabs of laddoos. How many crores of laddoos does it make?
activities.explanation: One arab is one hundred times one crore. So 5 arabs = 5*100 = 500 crores of laddoos.

lessons.title: Exact and Approximate Numbers

activities.prompt: When is a rounded number more helpful than an exact one?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Exact and Approximate Numbers
activities.body: Sometimes exact numbers are not needed, so an approximation is enough. Chintamani had exactly 76,068 people in 2011, but about 75,000 gives its size. Rounding up gives a greater number; rounding down gives a smaller number. A school with 732 people might need 750 sweets. A shopkeeper may call ₹470 around ₹450. For large numbers, nearest thousand, lakh or crore may help.
keyPoints: 76,068 is exact; about 75,000 is an approximation.
Rounding up gives a greater number; rounding down gives a smaller number.
Nearest thousand, lakh or crore may help for large numbers.
activities.explanation: Approximate numbers are useful when an exact number is not needed.

activities.prompt: A school with 732 people might need ______ sweets.
activities.hint: Think of a useful rounded-up amount.
activities.explanation: The school might need 750 sweets because it is greater than 732.

activities.prompt: Which amount is a useful rounded-up amount for 732 people?
activities.explanation: A school with 732 people might need 750 sweets.

activities.prompt: Ordering 750 sweets instead of 700 gives a useful rounded-up amount.
activities.explanation: Yes, 750 gives a useful rounded-up amount for the school.

activities.prompt: The exact population of Chintamani was 76,068. How many more people is this than an estimate of 75000 people?
activities.explanation: The exact count minus the estimate gives the difference: 76,068 - 75000 = 1068 people.

activities.prompt: A box has 48 full groups of 10 marbles and 1 extra marbles. After rounding down to the nearest 10, how many marbles does the estimate show?
activities.explanation: The extra marbles are left out, so 10 × 48 = 480 marbles.

activities.prompt: A basket has 37 full groups of 10 laddoos and 3 extra laddoos. After rounding up to the nearest 10, how many laddoos does the estimate show?
activities.explanation: There are extra laddoos, so the count is rounded to the next ten: 10 × (37 + 1) = 380 laddoos.

activities.prompt: A shopkeeper has 5 hundreds of rupees and 30 more rupees. He rounds the amount down to the nearest hundred. How many rupees does he say?
activities.explanation: The extra rupees are left out, so 100 × 5 = 500 rupees.

activities.prompt: Bengaluru's largest population increase was equal to 41,24,644.
activities.explanation: Bengaluru had the largest population increase, equal to 41,24,644.

activities.prompt: A city's population increase is 41 thousand and 800 more people, where 800 is between 500 and 999. What is the increase rounded to the nearest thousand?
activities.explanation: Because the extra part is at least 500, the increase rounds up to the next thousand: 1000 × (41 + 1) = 42000 people.

activities.prompt: A town's population is 4 lakh and 70000 more people, where 70000 is between 50,000 and 99,999. What is the population rounded to the nearest lakh?
activities.explanation: Because the extra part is at least 50,000, the population rounds up to the next lakh: 100000 × (4 + 1) = 500000 people.

lessons.title: Patterns in Products

activities.prompt: What shortcuts can make multiplying tricky numbers feel surprisingly simple?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Shortcuts and Digit Patterns
activities.body: Roxie multiplied 116 by 5 with a shortcut. She changed it into 58 × 10. Estu also used a shortcut for 824 × 25. Some products show interesting patterns in their digits. The number of digits in a product has clear limits. These limits depend on the numbers being multiplied.
keyPoints: Roxie changed 116 × 5 into 58 × 10.
Estu used a shortcut for 824 × 25.
Some products show interesting digit patterns.
Products have limits on their number of digits.
activities.explanation: Shortcut methods and digit-count rules help you spot useful patterns.

activities.prompt: Estu used a shortcut to multiply 824 by 25.
activities.explanation: Correct! Estu used a shortcut for 824 × 25.

activities.title: Complete Roxie's Multiplication
activities.prompt: Roxie used a shortcut to multiply 116 by ______.
activities.hint: Check the first multiplication in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Roxie's first shortcut was for 116 × 5.

activities.title: Possible Digit Counts
activities.prompt: Which digit counts are possible for a product of two 2-digit numbers?
activities.explanation: The product of two 2-digit numbers has 3 or 4 digits. Both counts are possible.

activities.title: Match the Product Rules
activities.prompt: Match each product rule with its detail.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a rule about the digit counts of products. Great matching!

activities.prompt: A box has 116 rows with 5 beads in each row. How many beads are in the box?
activities.explanation: Halve the number of rows and multiply by 10: (n/2)*10. This gives the total number of beads.

activities.prompt: A shop has 224 kg of apples. Each kg costs 25 rupees. What is the total cost in rupees?
activities.explanation: Since 25 = 100/4, use (n*100)/4 to find the total cost in rupees.

activities.prompt: A shop cuts 22 ropes into 11 pieces each. How many pieces are there in all?
activities.explanation: Multiply n*11. The products 121, 242, 363 and 484 show an interesting digit pattern.

activities.prompt: A 3-digit number is multiplied by a 4-digit number. What is the maximum number of digits in the product?
activities.explanation: The maximum number of digits in the product is the sum of the two digit counts: a+b.

activities.prompt: A 2-digit number is multiplied by a 2-digit number. What is the difference between the maximum and minimum possible numbers of digits in the product?
activities.explanation: The maximum is a+b and the minimum is a+b-1, so their difference is 1 digit.

activities.prompt: A shop puts 20 laddoos in each of 40 boxes. How many laddoos are there in all?
activities.explanation: Multiply the number of laddoos in each box by the number of boxes. Since both numbers have 2 digits, the product has either 3 or 4 digits.

activities.prompt: What can giant multiplications reveal about our world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Can a Large Number Tell Us?
activities.body: Here, “kīrtanas” means the compositions connected with Purandaradāsa. Multiplying 1250 by 380 gives their number. Large numbers can connect maths with space, nature, travel, waste, soil, cities, and paper. Calculations reveal an Earth–Sun distance, Amazon water flow, train travel, and plastic waste. Other results cover soil bacteria, bus capacity, Mumbai’s population, Titanic passengers, and paper weight. The Earth–Sun distance is approximate. Always ask what each number measures.
keyPoints: Kīrtanas are linked with Purandaradāsa’s compositions.
Different calculations reveal different kinds of information.
The Earth–Sun distance is approximate.
activities.explanation: Think about what each large number measures.

activities.title: Read the Meaning of Each Result
activities.body: One lakh buses can hold 50 lakh people. Mumbai had more than one crore 24 lakhs people. So its whole population cannot fit into one lakh buses. Dividing 13,95,000 by 150 gives the longest single-train journey distance. These examples show the need to read what a calculation measures.
keyPoints: One lakh buses hold 50 lakh people.
Mumbai’s whole population cannot fit into one lakh buses.
The train calculation gives a journey distance.
activities.explanation: A number may describe capacity, population, or distance.

activities.prompt: Purandaradāsa was only a painter in the 15th century.
activities.explanation: The lesson says Purandaradāsa was a composer and singer in the 15th century.

activities.prompt: What does dividing 13,95,000 by 150 reveal?
activities.explanation: Dividing 13,95,000 by 150 reveals the distance of the longest single-train journey.

activities.prompt: The plastic-waste calculation gives global plastic waste generated in 2021, in tonnes.
activities.explanation: This calculation gives the global plastic waste generated in 2021, measured in tonnes.

activities.explanation: Each pair connects an item with the result described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: The lesson multiplies 1250 kīrtanas by 500 to find Purandaradāsa's total. How many kīrtanas did this 15th-century composer and singer make?
The approximate distance from Earth to the Sun is found by multiplying 2200 by 80000. About how many million km is the distance?
activities.explanation: 2200 × 80000 = 2200 × 80000 km. Dividing by 1000000 gives 176 million km.

activities.prompt: The Amazon calculation gives an average of 125000 litres sent into the Atlantic each second. How many litres are sent in 600 seconds?
activities.explanation: Multiply the number of litres per second by the number of seconds: 125000 × 600 = 75000000 litres.

activities.prompt: The railway calculation divides 3000000 km by 150 to find the longest single-train journey. What distance in km does it give?
The plastic-waste calculation for 2021 gives 500 million tonnes of global plastic waste. How many lakh tonnes is that?
activities.explanation: 1 million tonnes equals 10 lakh tonnes, so 500 × 10 = 5000 lakh tonnes.

chapters.title: Arithmetic Expressions
chapters.summary: In this chapter: simple expressions; comparing expressions; reading and evaluating complex expressions; terms and the order of operations.

lessons.title: Simple Expressions

activities.prompt: Can different expressions have the same value?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is an expression?
activities.body: An arithmetic expression is a mathematical phrase, such as 13 + 2. Its value is the number it gives after you calculate. The expression 13 + 2 has the value 15. An equality sign shows how an expression connects with its value. You can write 13 + 2 = 15.
keyPoints: An expression is a mathematical phrase.
An expression has a value.
An equality sign connects an expression with its value.
activities.explanation: Expressions tell you how to combine numbers.

activities.title: Find the value
activities.prompt: What is the value of 13 + 2?
activities.explanation: 13 + 2 evaluates to 15.

activities.title: Match each one
activities.prompt: Match each expression or sign with its correct description.
pairs: shows the relationship between an expression and its value
activities.explanation: Each pair uses information given in the lesson.

activities.title: Same value
activities.prompt: The expressions 10 + 2 and 3 × 4 have the same value.
activities.explanation: Both expressions make twelve.

activities.title: Read the expression
activities.prompt: Which reading matches 5 × 25?
activities.explanation: 5 × 25 can be read as five times twenty-five.

activities.prompt: Riya has 5 marbles in one box and 4 marbles in another box. How many marbles are in the two boxes together?
activities.explanation: The total number of marbles is 5 + 4 = 9 marbles.

activities.prompt: Mallika's lunch costs 30 rupees a day. How much does she spend for 3 days in rupees?
activities.explanation: The total lunch cost is 3 * 30 = 90 rupees.

activities.prompt: Arun has 12 marbles. He gives 5 marbles to his friend. How many marbles does he have left?
activities.explanation: The number of marbles left is 12 - 5 = 7 marbles.

activities.prompt: 24 marbles are shared equally among 2 children. How many marbles does each child get?
activities.explanation: Each child gets 24 / 2 = 12 marbles.

activities.prompt: The equality shows the total number of marbles: 6 + 5 = ____.
activities.explanation: The value of the expression is 6 + 5 = 11 marbles.

lessons.title: Comparing Expressions

activities.prompt: Which expression has more marbles—and how can you tell?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Compare by finding values
activities.body: Expressions are compared using their values. First, find the value of each expression. Then say whether the first is greater than, less than, or equal to the second. For example, 10 + 2 has value 12, while 7 + 1 has value 8. So the first expression is greater. Marble stories can help you compare amounts.
keyPoints: Find the value of each expression.
Compare the two values.
Say greater, less, or equal.
activities.explanation: Find the values first, then compare them.

activities.title: Greater or less?
activities.prompt: Is 13 – 2 greater than 4 × 3?
activities.explanation: Not quite. 13 – 2 has value 11, while 4 × 3 has value 12.

activities.title: Match the comparisons
activities.prompt: Match each expression with its comparison.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a true comparison. Great matching!

activities.title: Raja's starting amount
activities.prompt: Raja begins with ______ marbles.
activities.hint: Think about the beginning of the marble situation.
activities.explanation: Good recall! Raja begins the marble situation with 1023 marbles.

activities.prompt: A tray has 4 rows with 6 laddoos in each row. How many laddoos are on the tray?
activities.explanation: The number of laddoos is 4 × 6 = 24 laddoos.

activities.prompt: One jar has 20 laddoos and another jar has 15 laddoos. How many more laddoos are in the larger jar?
activities.explanation: Compare the values and subtract the smaller value from the larger value: 20 − 15 = 5 laddoos.

activities.prompt: Raja has 18 marbles and gives away 2. Another group has 3*2 marbles. How many more marbles does Raja's group have than the other group?
activities.explanation: First find Raja's value, 18 − 2. Find the other group's value, 3 × 2. Then subtract to get the difference in marbles.

activities.prompt: Raja begins with 1021 marbles and receives 126 marbles. How many marbles does Raja have now?
activities.explanation: The number of marbles Raja has now is 1021 + 126 = 1147 marbles.

activities.prompt: Joy begins with 1022 marbles and receives 129. Raja begins with the same 1022 marbles and receives 124. How many more marbles does Joy have than Raja?
activities.explanation: Find Joy's value, 1022 + 129. Find Raja's value, 1022 + 124. Subtract Raja's value from Joy's value to find the difference in marbles.

activities.title: Order by value
activities.prompt: Put these expressions in order from smallest value to largest value.
activities.explanation: The values rise from 8 to 11 to 12. Great ordering!

activities.prompt: Raja has 111 marbles and loses 25 of them. How many marbles does Raja have left?
activities.explanation: The number of marbles Raja has left is 111 − 25 = 86 marbles.

lessons.title: Reading and Evaluating Complex Expressions

activities.prompt: Which operation should we tackle first when an expression gets confusing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Making the order clear
activities.body: An expression without a context can sometimes be evaluated in more than one way. In 30 + 5 × 4, the order is not clear. Brackets and terms remove confusion. Find values inside brackets before other operations. A bracketed expression may describe marbles brought. Another example says Irfan receives twenty-nine rupees as change.
keyPoints: Some expressions have unclear order.
Brackets help remove confusion.
Find bracketed values first.
activities.explanation: Clear working helps you understand how an expression should be evaluated.

activities.title: Why brackets matter
activities.body: First, look for brackets. The values inside them must be found before any other operations. The expression within the brackets is evaluated first. This makes the working clear. A bracketed expression can describe the number of marbles brought. Irfan also receives twenty-nine rupees as change in the lesson.
keyPoints: Brackets show which values come first.
Evaluate the expression within brackets first.
Clear working removes confusion.
activities.explanation: Brackets show the correct order and make each step easier to understand.

activities.title: A clear question
activities.prompt: The expression 30 + 5 × 4 does not clearly show which operation comes first.
activities.explanation: The expression does not clearly show whether to multiply or add first.

activities.title: Choose the first step
activities.prompt: What should happen first in 30 + 5 × 4?
activities.explanation: Multiply 5 and 4 first. Then add the product to 30.

activities.title: Match each part
activities.prompt: Match each part of the expression to its meaning.
activities.explanation: The two numbers are multiplied first. Their product is then added to 30.

activities.prompt: A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. What is its perimeter in cm?
activities.explanation: Find the sum of the length and width, then multiply by 2. For example, 2 x (8 + 5) = 26 cm.

activities.prompt: A shop has 3 loose laddoos and 4 packets with 5 laddoos in each packet. How many laddoos does the shop have?
activities.explanation: Multiply the number of laddoos in each packet by the number of packets, then add the loose laddoos. For example, 5 + 6 x 3 = 23 laddoos.

activities.prompt: There are 3 buses with 8 children in each bus and 10 children travelling in cars. How many children are travelling altogether?
activities.explanation: First find all the children in the buses, then add the children in the cars. For example, 5 x 10 + 6 = 56 children.

activities.prompt: A shop gives 7 loose laddoos and 5 boxes with 4 laddoos in each box. How many laddoos does the shop give?
activities.explanation: Multiply the number of laddoos in each box by the number of boxes, then add the loose laddoos. For example, 4 + 3 x 2 = 10 laddoos.

activities.prompt: A bus has 6 rows with 8 seats in each row. 10 seats are occupied. How many seats are empty?
activities.explanation: Find the total number of seats inside the brackets, then subtract the occupied seats. For example, (5 x 10) - 8 = 42 empty seats.

activities.title: Order the working
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to evaluate 30 + (5 × 4).
activities.explanation: Find the bracketed values first. Then multiply and add in the correct order.

activities.prompt: Irfan brings 7 bags and 4 extra bags, with 6 marbles in each bag. How many marbles does Irfan bring?
activities.explanation: Find the total number of bags inside the brackets, then multiply by the marbles in each bag. For example, (3 + 2) x 6 = 30 marbles.

lessons.title: Terms and the Order of Operations

activities.prompt: Ready to discover why rearranging an expression’s parts keeps the same answer?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Terms
activities.body: Terms are the parts of an expression separated by plus signs. When identifying terms, change every subtraction into addition. A multiplication part without a plus sign is one term. The inverse of a number has the opposite sign. Swapping terms keeps the sum unchanged. This is the commutative property. Grouping terms keeps the sum unchanged. This is the associative property. Evaluate multiplication or division first. Then add all evaluated terms.
keyPoints: Terms are separated by plus signs.
Swapping and grouping keep the sum unchanged.
Evaluate multiplication or division before adding terms.
activities.explanation: These rules help you identify and calculate with terms correctly.

activities.prompt: What are terms?
activities.explanation: Plus signs show where an expression's parts begin and end.

activities.prompt: All subtractions become additions when identifying terms.
activities.explanation: Identifying terms changes every subtraction into addition.

activities.prompt: The inverse of a number has the ______ sign.
activities.hint: Think about the sign of the number.
activities.explanation: An inverse changes a number's sign to the opposite sign.

activities.prompt: Which kind of part is one term?
options: Every plus sign left standing alone
activities.explanation: A multiplication part without a plus sign stays as one term.

activities.prompt: Match each description to its mathematical name.
pairs: A number with the opposite sign
Swapping terms without changing the sum
Grouping terms without changing the sum
activities.explanation: Each description matches the rule for terms, inverses, swapping, or grouping.

activities.prompt: Which parts are evaluated before the terms are added?
activities.explanation: Terms with multiplication or division are evaluated before the final addition.

activities.prompt: Put the evaluation steps in the correct order.
activities.explanation: Evaluate multiplication or division first. Then finish evaluating the terms and add them.

activities.prompt: Which pair of actions keeps the sum unchanged?
activities.explanation: Both swapping terms and grouping terms keep the sum unchanged.

activities.prompt: A shopkeeper has 47 marbles and gives away 14 marbles. How many marbles remain?
activities.explanation: Subtracting b is the same as adding its inverse, so a+(-b) gives the number of marbles remaining.

activities.prompt: There are 9 boxes with 6 laddoos in each box, and 3 extra laddoos. How many laddoos are there altogether?
activities.explanation: The multiplication part a*b is one term. It is evaluated before c is added.

activities.prompt: A child has 16 marbles, 5 marbles, and 17 marbles in three piles. What is the total if the piles are added in the order 17, 16, 5?
activities.explanation: When there are only additions, the terms can be added in any order, so c+a+b gives the total number of marbles.

lessons.title: More Expressions and Their Terms

activities.prompt: How can numbers show what we combine, add, or separate?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Expressions and Their Terms
activities.body: Ruby’s expression has two terms: 6 × 5 and 3. Together, they mean three more than 6 × 5. The cost of four dosas at 23 rupees each is shown as 4 × 23. Another expression, 100 ÷ 2, shows the number of new two-kilogram packets. His total combines four existing packets with 100 ÷ 2 new packets. There is more than one way to pay 432 rupees.
keyPoints: Ruby’s expression has two terms.
6 × 5 and 3 mean three more than 6 × 5.
4 × 23 shows the cost of four dosas.
activities.explanation: These expressions connect real situations with numbers and terms.

activities.prompt: The cost of four dosas at 23 rupees each is written as 4 + 23.
activities.explanation: The cost is written as 4 × 23, not 4 + 23.

activities.prompt: Which are the two terms in Ruby’s expression?
activities.explanation: Ruby’s expression is written as the two terms 6 × 5 and 3.

activities.prompt: Match each expression with what it shows in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each expression is paired with the situation it shows.

activities.prompt: A shop sells 4 dosas at 23 rupees each. What is the total cost in rupees?
activities.explanation: Total cost = n * p. For example, 4 * 23 = 92 rupees.

activities.prompt: Ruby has 5 rows of 7 marbles and adds 5 more marbles. How many marbles does she have in all?
activities.explanation: Ruby first has a * b marbles. Adding c more gives a * b + c. For example, 4 * 5 + 3 = 23 marbles.

activities.prompt: There are 100 kilograms of marbles. Each packet holds 5 kilograms. How many packets can be made?
activities.explanation: Divide the total kilograms by the kilograms in each packet. For example, 100 / 2 = 50 packets.

activities.prompt: His total number of packets combines four existing packets with 100 ÷ 2 new packets.
activities.explanation: Yes, his total combines four existing packets with the new packets.

activities.prompt: A shop has 5 packets already. It makes 40 kilograms of new packets, with 5 kilograms in each packet. How many packets are there altogether?
activities.explanation: First find the number of new packets by dividing k by w. Then add e. For example, 4 + 100 / 2 = 54 packets.

activities.prompt: Neha can pay 432 rupees in more than one way. One way uses 1 100-rupee notes and 3 20-rupee notes. What is the total value of these notes in rupees?
activities.explanation: Multiply the number of notes by the value of each note, and then add. For example, 2 * 100 + 3 * 20 = 260 rupees.

lessons.title: Removing Brackets and Distributing Multiplication

activities.prompt: Can we make these tricky brackets disappear without changing the answer?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Removing Brackets
activities.body: Brackets are removed by looking at the sign just before them. After a minus sign, change every sign inside the brackets. After a plus sign, keep every sign inside the brackets. For example, 500 – (250 – 100) becomes 500 – 250 + 100. This shows how signs change when brackets are removed.
keyPoints: A minus sign changes every inner sign.
A plus sign keeps every inner sign.
activities.explanation: The sign before the brackets tells you how to change the inner signs.

activities.prompt: Removing brackets after a plus sign keeps the signs of the terms inside.
activities.explanation: Correct. A plus sign does not change the signs inside the brackets.

activities.prompt: In 500 – (250 – 100), the sign of 250 becomes ______.
activities.hint: The minus sign before the brackets changes both inner signs.
activities.explanation: The minus sign makes 250 negative and 100 positive.

activities.prompt: Which expression has the same value as 100 – (15 + 56)?
activities.explanation: Removing the minus sign gives 100 – 15 – 56. Both expressions have the same value.

activities.prompt: Match each bracketed expression with its equal form.
activities.explanation: After a minus sign, change the inner signs. This gives each matching expression.

activities.title: Distributing Multiplication
activities.body: Multiplication can be distributed over a sum. The multiple of a sum is the same as the sum of the multiples. So 5 × (4 + 3) becomes 5 × 4 + 5 × 3. Also, 10 × 98 + 3 × 98 equals 13 × 98. These equalities help us work with multiplication.
keyPoints: Distribute 5 across 4 + 3.
The multiple of a sum equals the sum of multiples.
activities.explanation: Distributing multiplication keeps the expression equal while making the products visible.

activities.prompt: The expression 5 × 4 + 3 is equal to 5 × (4 + 3).
activities.explanation: These expressions have different values. Distributing gives 5 × 4 + 5 × 3.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for changing 97 × 25 in order.
activities.explanation: Writing 97 as 100 – 3 lets you split the product into two multiples.

activities.prompt: Which expression correctly changes 63 × 18?
activities.explanation: Writing 63 as 53 + 10 gives 53 × 18 + 10 × 18.

activities.prompt: Ravi has 60 rupees. He spends 15 rupees on fruit and 10 rupees on sweets. How many rupees does he have left?
activities.explanation: The minus sign changes the signs of both terms inside the brackets, so the formula is cash-(cost+more). For the first listed values, the answer is 35 rupees.

activities.prompt: Riya has 50 marbles. She takes away 20 marbles and then puts back 5 marbles. How many marbles does she have now?
activities.explanation: Removing the outer bracket changes the signs to total-small+large. For the first listed values, the answer is 35 marbles.

activities.prompt: A shop earns ten times 98 rupees in the morning and three times 98 rupees in the afternoon. How many rupees does it earn altogether?
activities.explanation: Ten times the amount plus three times the amount is thirteen times the amount. For the first listed value, the answer is 1274 rupees.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: smaller units and tenths; hundredths and more precise lengths; decimal place value; converting units of measurement.

lessons.title: Smaller Units and Tenths

activities.prompt: Can tiny measurements help us solve a puzzling fitting problem?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Smaller Units
activities.body: The scale divides each unit between consecutive numbers into ten equal parts. Each small part is one-tenth, which means one of ten equal parts. Ten one-tenths make one whole unit. A length of 2 7 cm is two and seven-tenth centimetres. A length of 3 2 cm is three and two-tenth centimetres. Smaller units help us make more exact measurements.
keyPoints: Each unit divides into ten equal parts.
One-tenth means one of ten equal parts.
Smaller units make measurements more exact.
activities.explanation: These smaller parts help us write and compare exact lengths.

activities.title: The First Screw
activities.prompt: Why did the first screw not fit?
options: It was not the right size.
activities.explanation: The first screw did not fit because it was not the right size.

activities.prompt: The scale divides each unit between consecutive numbers into ten equal parts.
activities.explanation: Each unit is split into ten equal parts on the scale.

activities.title: Match Lengths with Words
activities.prompt: Match each length with its written form.
activities.explanation: Each length matches its written form in the lesson.

activities.prompt: The scale has 10 one-tenths in each whole unit. How many one-tenths are in 4 whole units?
activities.explanation: 10 x 4 = 10*n one-tenths.

activities.prompt: A pencil is 2 whole units and 8 one-tenths long. How many one-tenths long is the pencil?
activities.explanation: 10 x 2 + 8 = 10*w+t one-tenths.

activities.prompt: A length is 24 one-tenths long. How many one-tenths remain after 1 whole unit is made?
activities.explanation: Subtract 10 one-tenths for the whole unit: 24 - 10 = n-10 one-tenths.

activities.prompt: A screw is 25 one-tenths cm long. A USB cable is 30 one-tenths cm long. How many one-tenths cm longer is the cable?
activities.explanation: 30 - 25 = b-a one-tenths cm.

activities.prompt: A cable has 4 one-tenths of a unit and a pencil has 3 one-tenths of a unit. How many one-tenths of a unit do they have together?
activities.explanation: Add the two lengths: 4 + 3 = x+y one-tenths of a unit.

activities.title: Change Thirteen One-Tenths
activities.prompt: Put the steps for changing thirteen one-tenths into a larger unit.
items: One whole unit and three one-tenths
activities.explanation: First, take ten one-tenths. Then rename them as one whole unit.

activities.prompt: A screw is 2 and 7 cm long. A cable is 3 and 1 cm long. How many one-tenths cm longer is the cable?
activities.explanation: Write both lengths in one-tenths: 30 + 1 - (20 + 7) = (30+d)-(20+b) one-tenths cm.

lessons.title: Hundredths and More Precise Lengths

activities.prompt: How could tiny hundredths help us measure lengths more precisely?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Parts of a Whole
activities.body: Each one-tenth can be split into ten smaller parts. One whole unit has 100 smaller parts. Each smaller part is one-hundredth of a unit. Ten one-hundredths make one one-tenth. We can use these parts to write lengths in different ways.
keyPoints: One whole unit has 100 smaller parts.
Each smaller part is one-hundredth of a unit.
Ten one-hundredths make one one-tenth.
activities.explanation: Hundredths help us write lengths more precisely.

activities.title: Build a decimal

tasks.then: 5 tenths is more than 5 hundredths, so 1.50 is bigger.

activities.takeaway: Each place is ten times the place to its right.
activities.explanation: Each place is ten times the place to its right.

activities.prompt: There are 100 smaller parts in one whole unit.
activities.explanation: One whole unit contains 100 smaller parts.

activities.prompt: Each smaller part is ______ of a unit.
activities.hint: There are 100 smaller parts in one whole unit.
activities.explanation: Each smaller part is one-hundredth of a unit.

activities.prompt: What do ten one-hundredths make?
activities.explanation: Ten one-hundredths make one one-tenth.

activities.prompt: There are 2 whole laddoos. If each laddoo is cut into one-hundredth pieces, how many one-hundredth pieces are there altogether?
activities.explanation: Each whole laddoo has 100 one-hundredth pieces, so 2 whole laddoos have 2 * 100 one-hundredth pieces.

activities.prompt: A ribbon is 2 tenths of a metre long. How many hundredths of a metre long is it?
activities.explanation: Each one-tenth has 10 one-hundredths, so 2 tenths have 2 * 10 hundredths.

activities.prompt: A bus travels 20 hundredths of a kilometre. How many tenths of a kilometre does the bus travel?
activities.explanation: Ten one-hundredths make one one-tenth, so divide 20 hundredths by 10 to find the number of tenths.

activities.prompt: A bus fare is one whole rupee and 5 tenths of a rupee. How many hundredths of a rupee is the fare?
activities.explanation: One whole rupee is 100 hundredths, and each one-tenth is 10 hundredths. The fare is 100 + 5 * 10 hundredths.

activities.prompt: A red ribbon is 50 hundredths of a metre long. A blue ribbon is 2 tenths of a metre long. How many more hundredths of a metre long is the red ribbon?
activities.explanation: First change 2 tenths into 2 * 10 hundredths. Then subtract that from 50 hundredths.

activities.prompt: Put these lengths from largest to smallest.
activities.explanation: One whole unit contains 100 hundredths. One-tenth contains 10 hundredths.

activities.prompt: A ribbon is one tenth of a metre and 5 hundredths of a metre long. How many hundredths of a metre long is it?
activities.explanation: One tenth is 10 hundredths, so adding 5 hundredths gives 10 + 5 hundredths.

lessons.title: Decimal Place Value

activities.prompt: What does one little dot tell us about a number?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Reading decimal place value
activities.body: Decimal place value helps you read numbers by place. The decimal point separates whole numbers from fractional parts. Each place value is ten times bigger than the place to its right. One-tenths come from dividing one into ten equal parts. One-hundredths come from dividing a tenth into ten parts. In 70.5, the 7 is in the tens place and the 5 is in the tenths place.
keyPoints: The decimal point separates whole numbers from fractional parts.
Each place value is ten times bigger than the place to its right.
One-tenths and one-hundredths are parts of a whole unit.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you read decimals clearly.

activities.title: Build a decimal

tasks.then: 5 tenths is more than 5 hundredths, so 1.50 is bigger.

activities.takeaway: Each place is ten times the place to its right.
activities.explanation: Each place is ten times the place to its right.

activities.title: Find the tens and tenths
activities.prompt: Which number has 7 in the tens place and 5 in the tenths place?
activities.explanation: 70.5 means 7 tens and 5 tenths.

activities.title: Check the statement
activities.prompt: The number 7.05 means 7 units and 5 hundredths.
activities.explanation: Yes, 7.05 has 7 units and 5 hundredths.

activities.title: Complete the place value
activities.prompt: The number 705 means 7 ______ and 5 ones.
activities.hint: Think about the place before ones.
activities.explanation: 705 means 7 hundreds and 5 ones.

activities.title: Match numbers and meanings
activities.prompt: Match each number with its place value meaning.
pairs: A special number in the Indian place value system
activities.explanation: Each matching pair shows a number and its place value meaning.

activities.prompt: Each of 5 laddoos is split into 4 equal parts. How many equal parts are there altogether?

activities.prompt: Each of 5 laddoos is split into 4 equal parts, and each part is split into 4 equal parts. How many smallest parts are there altogether?
activities.explanation: Each laddoo makes 4*4 equal parts, so n*4*4 smallest parts are made.

activities.prompt: A ribbon is 8 cm long. How many tenths of a centimetre long is it?
activities.explanation: One centimetre has 10 tenths of a centimetre, so n*10 tenths of a centimetre make the ribbon's length.

activities.prompt: A piece of ribbon is 7 tenths of a centimetre long. How many hundredths of a centimetre long is it?
activities.explanation: One tenth has 10 hundredths, so n*10 hundredths of a centimetre make the ribbon's length.

activities.prompt: A money box has 4 ten-rupee notes and 2 tenths of a rupee. How many rupees are there altogether?
activities.explanation: The 4 tens give 10*n rupees, and the 2 tenths give t/10 rupees, so 10*n+t/10 gives the total in rupees.

activities.prompt: A pencil is 4 units long and 10 hundredths of a unit extra. How many units long is the pencil?
activities.explanation: The whole part is u units and the fractional part is h/100 units, so u+h/100 gives the pencil's length in units.

lessons.title: Converting Units of Measurement

activities.prompt: How can we turn tiny millimetres into whole metres?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Changing between units
activities.body: A millimetre is a small length unit. One centimetre has the length of 10 millimetres. Multiply centimetres by 10 to get millimetres. Divide millimetres by 10 to get centimetres. One metre is 100 centimetres. One kilogram is a mass unit. It equals 1,000 grams. For money, 1 rupee equals 100 paise. These equalities help you change units.
keyPoints: 1 centimetre = 10 millimetres
1 metre = 100 centimetres
1 kilogram = 1000 grams
activities.explanation: These equalities let you change measurements into other units.

activities.prompt: One centimetre equals 0.1 millimetre.
activities.explanation: One centimetre equals 10 millimetres. One millimetre equals 0.1 centimetre.

activities.title: Change centimetres into millimetres

activities.hint: Use the rule for changing centimetres into millimetres.

activities.title: Find the matching length

activities.title: Match each unit to its equal
activities.prompt: Match each unit on the left with its equal on the right.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows equal amounts of two related units.

activities.prompt: A marble is 20 mm long. What is its length in centimetres?

activities.prompt: A red ribbon is 1 cm long. What is its length in millimetres?
activities.explanation: Centimetres multiplied by 10 gives millimetres: n*10 mm. The answers are 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 mm.

activities.prompt: A small bus is 1 m long. What is its length in centimetres?
activities.explanation: Metres multiplied by 100 gives centimetres: n*100 cm. The answers are 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 cm.

activities.prompt: A bag of laddoos weighs 1 kg. What is its weight in grams?

activities.prompt: A toy bus costs 5 rupees. What is its cost in paise?
activities.explanation: Rupees multiplied by 100 gives paise: n*100 paise. The answers are 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 paise.

activities.body: Decimals have place values. The number 1.4 means 1 unit and 4 tenths, so it lies between 1 and 2. Compare decimals by starting with their highest place values. At the first different place, the larger digit gives the greater number. The numbers 0.2, 0.02 and 0.002 have different values, although adding zeros on the right does not change 0.2. The divisions between 1 and 1.1 are hundredths.

Compare decimals from their highest place values
0.2, 0.02 and 0.002 have different values
activities.explanation: These ideas will help you locate and compare decimals.

tasks.then: 5 tenths is more than 5 hundredths, so 1.50 is bigger.

activities.prompt: The number 1.4 lies between 1 and 2.

activities.title: Divisions Between 1 and 1.1

activities.prompt: A packet of sweets costs ₹2.5. How many rupees is the total cost?
activities.explanation: ₹2.5 has 2 whole rupees and 5 tenths of a rupee, so the total is 2 + 5/10 = 2.5 rupees.

activities.prompt: A bus fare is ₹3.50. It lies between ₹3 and the next whole number. How many rupees is it above ₹3?
activities.explanation: The fare is 50 hundredths above ₹3. Thus, (3 + 50/100) - 3 = 0.5 rupees.

activities.prompt: Two marks on a ruler are 1 cm and 1.2 cm apart. The gap is divided into hundredths. How many one-hundredth intervals are there?
activities.explanation: There are 10 hundredths in one tenth, so the number of one-hundredth intervals is 10 * 2 = 20.

activities.prompt: A toy bus costs ₹5. A shopkeeper writes the price as ₹5.00. What is the price in rupees?
activities.explanation: The zeros on the right do not change the value. Therefore, ₹5.00 = 5 + 0/10 + 0/100 = 5 rupees.

activities.prompt: Three packets are marked ₹0.5, ₹0.05, and ₹0.005. What is the value in rupees of the marking with the greatest value?
activities.explanation: The marking ₹0.5 has the greatest value. Its value is 5/10 = 0.5 rupees.

lessons.title: Adding Decimals and Avoiding Decimal Mistakes

activities.prompt: How can one tiny decimal point make such a big difference?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Decimals and the decimal point
activities.body: Decimals can be added or subtracted using the same method as whole numbers. Line up decimal points and keep each digit in the correct column. A decimal point separates whole and fractional parts. Priya and Shylaja together need 6.2 metres of cloth. Read medicine amounts carefully: 0.05 mg is not 0.5 mg. Today, the decimal point is the most popular notation for fractional numbers.
keyPoints: Add decimals using the whole-number method.
Line up decimal points carefully.
Check decimal points before calculating.
activities.explanation: Careful columns and careful decimal points help prevent mistakes.

activities.prompt: Reading 0.05 mg as 0.5 mg can give ten times the prescribed medicine.
activities.explanation: The small change from 0.05 mg to 0.5 mg can cause this danger.

activities.prompt: How many minutes equal 0.5 hours?
activities.explanation: The time 0.5 hours is equal to 30 minutes.

activities.prompt: Put these terms in order. Each term comes after adding 0.4.
activities.explanation: Start with 0.4. Add 0.4 each time to reach the next term.

activities.prompt: An account of a detailed modern form of decimal notation appeared around 950 CE. In 15.4, how many tenths are in the fractional part?
activities.explanation: The decimal point separates the whole and fractional parts. The digit 4 after the point shows 4 tenths, so the answer is 4 tenths.

activities.prompt: One child has 30.50 rupees and another child has 10.25 rupees. How many rupees do they have altogether?
activities.explanation: Line up the decimal points and add: 30.50 + 10.25 = 30 + 10 + 0.75 = 40.75 rupees.

activities.prompt: A sequence starts with 1, and adding 0.4 gives the next term. What is the next term?
activities.explanation: Add 0.4 to the first term: 1 + 0.4 = 1.4.

activities.prompt: A detailed modern form of decimal notation appeared around 950 CE.
activities.explanation: The detailed modern form was described in an account from around 950 CE.

activities.prompt: A bus trip takes 1.5 hours. How many minutes is that?
activities.explanation: Each whole hour has 60 minutes, and 0.5 hours is 30 minutes. Therefore, 1.5 hours = 1 x 60 + 30 = 90 minutes.

activities.prompt: A medicine label says 1.05 mg, but it is read as 1.5 mg. How many extra mg are given?
activities.explanation: Subtract the prescribed dose from the wrongly read dose: 1.5 - 1.05 = 1 x 0.45 = 0.45 extra mg.

activities.prompt: A child writes 2.6 feet for a door that is 2 feet 6 inches tall. How many inches is the part after the decimal point meant to show?
activities.explanation: The part after the decimal point is meant to show the inches. Therefore, it should show 6 inches, so the answer is 6.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Letter-Numbers and Algebraic Expressions

activities.prompt: How can we use letters to solve age, counting, and cost puzzles?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Using letters for numbers
activities.body: Letter-numbers give a short way to show relationships and patterns. Letters such as a and s can stand for numbers. The expression a + 3 shows Shabnam's age when a is Aftab's age. If a is 23, s is 26 years. Matchstick examples use 2 × n, while shopping costs use c × 35 + j × 60.
keyPoints: Letters can represent numbers.
Algebraic expressions show relationships.
Different expressions describe different situations.
activities.explanation: Letters help us show number relationships clearly and quickly.

activities.title: Expressions for different situations
activities.body: Algebraic expressions connect letters with numbers to describe situations. For ages, a + 3 finds Shabnam's age from Aftab's age. The reverse relation is a = s – 3. For matchsticks, 2 × n gives the total when there are n Ls. For shopping, c × 35 + j × 60 gives the total cost.
keyPoints: a + 3 gives Shabnam's age.
2 × n gives the number of matchsticks.
c × 35 + j × 60 gives the total cost.
activities.explanation: Each algebraic expression represents a particular relationship.

activities.prompt: The expression a + 3 is an algebraic expression.
activities.explanation: It uses a letter and a number to show a relationship.

activities.prompt: What is the value of s when a is 23?
activities.explanation: Adding 3 to 23 gives s = 26 years.

activities.prompt: The letter-number m stands for the number of laddoos on a plate. There are 20 laddoos. What number does m stand for?
activities.explanation: The letter-number m represents the given number of laddoos. Substituting m = 20, the answer is 20 laddoos.

activities.prompt: Aftab is 5 years old. Shabnam’s age is found by adding 3 to Aftab’s age. How old is Shabnam in years?
activities.explanation: Shabnam’s age is a + 3. Substituting a = 5, the answer is 8 years.

activities.prompt: Shabnam is 12 years old. Aftab’s age is 3 less than Shabnam’s age. How old is Aftab in years?
activities.explanation: Aftab’s age is s - 3. Substituting s = 12, the answer is 9 years.

activities.prompt: Match each situation with its correct expression or result.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a situation with its matching expression or result.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order for finding Shabnam's age when Aftab is 23.
activities.explanation: Start with Aftab's age, add 3, and find Shabnam's age.

activities.prompt: Each capital L needs 2 matchsticks. There are 3 Ls. How many matchsticks are needed?
activities.explanation: Multiply the number of Ls by 2: 2*n. Substituting n = 3, the answer is 6 matchsticks.

activities.prompt: A shopkeeper has 2 coconuts and 3 kg of jaggery. Each coconut costs 35 rupees and each kg of jaggery costs 60 rupees. What is the total cost in rupees?
activities.explanation: The total cost is c*35+j*60. Substituting c = 2 and j = 3, the answer is 250 rupees.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Revisiting Arithmetic Expressions

activities.prompt: Can changing the order or grouping of numbers change their total?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Rules for Expressions
activities.body: Swapping lets you add two numbers in any order. Grouping lets you add numbers in a convenient group. Neither change alters an expression’s value. You can use brackets with a negative sign outside. Brackets can be removed appropriately. A multiple of a sum equals the sum of its multiples. Before adding, turn every multiplication term into a number. Algebraic expressions take values when you replace their letters.
keyPoints: Swap numbers in any order.
Group terms conveniently.
Keep the expression’s value.
activities.explanation: These rules help you simplify expressions without changing their value.

activities.prompt: Swapping and grouping do not change the value of an expression.
activities.explanation: You can swap or group the terms and keep the same value.

activities.prompt: Grouping terms does not change the ______ of an expression.
activities.hint: Think about what stays the same.
activities.explanation: Grouping adds numbers conveniently without changing the expression’s value.

activities.prompt: Match each idea to its meaning.
pairs: Adding two numbers in any order
Adding numbers in a convenient way
A multiple of a sum equals a sum of multiples
Can have a negative sign outside
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an expression rule with its correct meaning.

activities.prompt: A multiplication term must become a number before you add it.
activities.explanation: Convert every term containing a multiplication sign into a number before adding.

activities.prompt: A negative sign can appear outside brackets.
activities.explanation: Brackets may have a negative sign outside. They can also be removed appropriately.

activities.prompt: Put these steps for replacing a in s = a + 3 in order.
activities.explanation: Replacing a with 23 gives s = 23 + 3 = 26 years.

activities.prompt: A bag costs 15 rupees and a lunch box costs 7 rupees. Swapping their order gives the same total. What is the total in rupees?
activities.explanation: Swapping the two prices does not change their sum. The total is 15+7 rupees.

activities.prompt: A shop multiplies the sum of a 8-rupee item and a 6-rupee item by 3. What is the total in rupees after removing the brackets?
activities.explanation: Removing the brackets gives 3*8+3*6, which is the total in rupees.

activities.prompt: Replacing a by 22 in s=a+3 gives s. What is s in years?
activities.explanation: Replace a with the given number and add 3. When a is 23, s is 23+3=26 years.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Omitting the Multiplication Symbol

activities.prompt: Can you discover what happens when we leave out the multiplication sign?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Leaving Out the Multiplication Sign
activities.body: The sequence 4, 8, 12 and onwards contains the multiples of 4. Here, n shows a position in the sequence. The nth term means the term at position n. Its value is 4 times n. This rule is shortened from 4 × n to 4n. A number before a letter means multiplication, so 5m means 5 × m. Also, 7k means 7 × k.
keyPoints: n shows a position in the sequence
4n means 4 × n
5m means 5 × m
activities.explanation: Leaving out the sign still keeps the multiplication meaning.

activities.prompt: The sequence 4, 8, 12 and onwards contains the multiples of 4.
activities.explanation: This sequence contains the multiples of 4.

activities.prompt: The letter ______ shows a position in the sequence.
activities.hint: It marks a place in the sequence.
activities.explanation: The letter n shows a position in the sequence.

activities.prompt: What does 5m mean?
activities.explanation: A number before a letter means multiplication.

activities.prompt: Which expression gives the third term?
activities.explanation: The third term is found by multiplying 4 by 3.

activities.prompt: Match each expression with its meaning from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each expression shows a term or a value from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these sequence positions in order from earliest to latest.
activities.explanation: The third term comes before the twenty-ninth term.

activities.prompt: When m = 2, what is the value of 5m + 3?
activities.explanation: When m = 2, the value of 5m + 3 is 13.

activities.prompt: The nth term is written as ______n when the multiplication sign is left out.
activities.hint: Use the value of 4 times n.
activities.explanation: The nth term is 4 times n. Leaving out the multiplication sign gives 4n.

activities.prompt: A shop arranges laddoos in groups of 4, 8, 12, and so on. If one group has 4 laddoos, how many laddoos are in the next group?
activities.explanation: (t+4) gives the number of laddoos in the next group. For t = 4, the answer is 8 laddoos.

activities.prompt: A bus stand needs 7 tyres for each bus. If there are 3 buses, how many tyres are needed?
activities.explanation: (7*k) gives the number of tyres needed for k buses. For k = 3, the answer is 21 tyres.

activities.prompt: There are 5 marbles in each of m groups, and 3 marbles are left over. If m = 2, how many marbles are there altogether?
activities.explanation: (5*m+3) gives the total number of marbles. For m = 2, the answer is 13 marbles.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Simplifying Algebraic Expressions

activities.prompt: Ready to discover how to make a long expression shorter without changing its value?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Simplifying Expressions
activities.body: A rectangle’s perimeter can start as length + breadth + length + breadth. Using l and b, we write p = l + b + l + b. Like terms have the same letter-numbers, so this becomes p = 2l + 2b. Both forms take the same values. Terms with different letter-numbers are unlike terms. Adding 5c, 3c and 10c uses the distributive property and gives 18c. Similarly, 4v + 3v gives 7v.
keyPoints: p = l + b + l + b becomes p = 2l + 2b.
Like terms have the same letter-numbers.
Unlike terms have different letter-numbers.
activities.explanation: You have spotted how to combine terms without changing the value.

activities.prompt: Which expression shows a rectangle's perimeter before simplification?
activities.explanation: The original perimeter expression lists the length and breadth twice.

activities.prompt: The expressions l + b + l + b and 2l + 2b take the same values.
activities.explanation: Both expressions give the same values for the same length and breadth.

activities.prompt: When l = 3 and b = 4, both perimeter expressions give ______.
activities.explanation: Both perimeter expressions give 14 when l = 3 and b = 4.

activities.prompt: Which pair contains like terms?
activities.explanation: The terms 4v and 3v have the same letter-number, v.

activities.prompt: The smaller areas 4v and 3v add to 7v.
activities.explanation: The lesson adds the smaller areas 4v and 3v to get 7v.

activities.prompt: Why can 18c + 11d not be simplified further?
activities.explanation: The expression has different letter-numbers, so it cannot simplify further.

activities.prompt: Match each expression with its simplified form.
activities.explanation: Like terms combine to make the matching simplified expression.

activities.prompt: Put the pencil expression in order from the combined c terms to the full expression.
activities.explanation: The three c terms combine first, and then 11d remains.

activities.prompt: A rectangle is 3 cm long and 4 cm wide, where 3=3 and 4=4. What is its perimeter in cm?
activities.explanation: Perimeter = l + b + l + b = 2*(l+b) = 2*(3+4) = 14 cm.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Finding Formulas and Describing Patterns

activities.prompt: Can we discover a hidden rule and turn it into a formula?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Describe, Then Formula
activities.body: First describe a relationship in simple words. Then write it as an expression. Here, nth means the number in a counting sequence. The number-machine rule is two times the first number minus the second number, so its expression is 2a – b. For repeating designs, use nth occurrences to find positions. Design C is at 3n. Designs B and A are at 3n – 1 and 3n – 2.
keyPoints: Describe relationships simply.
The number-machine rule is 2a – b.
Use nth formulas to find design positions.
activities.explanation: Simple words help you understand a formula before writing it.

activities.prompt: Which expression shows the number-machine rule?
activities.explanation: The rule doubles the first number, then subtracts the second number.

activities.prompt: The number-machine rule adds the second number to two times the first.
activities.explanation: No. It subtracts the second number from two times the first.

activities.prompt: The first input pair gives ______.
activities.hint: Use the number-machine rule with 5 and 2.
activities.explanation: Using 2 × 5 – 2 gives 8.

activities.prompt: Match each nth-position expression to its design.
activities.explanation: Each formula gives the position of that design's nth occurrence.

activities.prompt: Which design occurs at position 8?
activities.explanation: Position 8 appears in Design B's listed positions.

activities.prompt: Put the designs in order of their first occurrences.
activities.explanation: Their first positions are 1, 2 and 3, in that order.

activities.prompt: A position that is one less than a multiple of 3 has Design B.
activities.explanation: Yes. Such positions have Design B.

activities.prompt: A position is 2 less than a multiple of 3. Which design has that position?
activities.explanation: A position two less than a multiple of 3 has Design A.

activities.prompt: A machine doubles 6 marbles and then subtracts 4 marbles. How many marbles are left?
activities.explanation: Double 6, then subtract 4: 2*6-4=8 marbles.

activities.prompt: The first input pair 5 and 2 makes 8 laddoos because 2 × 5 – 2 = 8. If the machine is checked 4 times, how many laddoos does it make in all?
activities.explanation: Each run makes 8 laddoos. For 4 runs, the total is 32 laddoos.

activities.prompt: Design C is placed at every third spot in a row. At which numbered spot does the nth Design C appear?
activities.explanation: The positions of Design C are 3, 6, 9, 12 and so on. For n=1, the position is 3.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Calendar and Matchstick Patterns

activities.prompt: Can you discover the calendar’s secret and predict how many matchsticks come next?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Calendar diagonals and matchstick patterns
activities.body: A diagonal means a slanting line. The marked calendar square has 12, 20, 13 and 19 on its diagonals. If a is the centre, its opposite number is 8 more. The number below is 7 more. Both diagonal sums equal 2a + 8. The five-number total is 5 times its centre. In the matchstick pattern, Step 5 needs 11 matchsticks. Each new step adds 2.
keyPoints: The two diagonal sums are equal.
The matchstick count is 3 + 2 × (y – 1).
This equals 2y + 1.
activities.explanation: These rules help you solve both calendar and matchstick patterns.

activities.prompt: Which number is diagonally opposite 12?
activities.explanation: The marked diagonal pairs 12 with 20. This confirms the opposite number.

activities.prompt: The two diagonal sums are equal for every value of a.
activities.explanation: Both sums simplify to 2a + 8. They match for every value of a.

activities.prompt: The number below a is ______ more than it.
activities.explanation: The rule says that the number below a is 7 more. This matches the blank.

activities.prompt: What is the total of the five-number shape?
activities.explanation: The total is the centre number multiplied by 5. So the total is 5a.

activities.prompt: Match each starting number or phrase to its match.
activities.explanation: The marked diagonal pairs are 12 with 20 and 13 with 19. The other pairs follow the calendar rules.

activities.prompt: How many matchsticks are needed at Step 5?
activities.explanation: The pattern tells us that Step 5 needs 11 matchsticks. You found the correct count.

activities.prompt: At Step 3, the count is 3 + 2 × (3 – 1) = ______.
activities.explanation: Multiplying 2 by 2 gives 4. Adding 3 gives 7 matchsticks.

activities.prompt: Put these matchstick stages in order from the first step to the last step.
activities.explanation: Each new step adds 2 matchsticks. The counts therefore rise from 3 to 5 to 11.

activities.prompt: On the marked calendar square, the number diagonally opposite 5 is 8 more. What is the diagonally opposite calendar number?
activities.explanation: The opposite number is 5 + 8. For example, when 5 = 12, the answer is 20.

activities.prompt: The centre number of a five-number shape is 2. What is the total of the five calendar numbers in the shape?
activities.explanation: The total is 5 * 2. For example, when 2 = 4, the answer is 20.

activities.prompt: Step 5 of a matchstick pattern uses 11 matchsticks. How many more matchsticks are used at Step 7 than at Step 5?
activities.explanation: Two more matchsticks are added at each new step, so the difference is 2*(7 - 5). For example, Step 8 uses 6 more matchsticks.

lessons.title: 5.1 Across the Line

activities.prompt: Can you solve the missing-angle puzzle created by two crossing lines?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet at One Point
activities.body: Intersecting lines meet at one point on a plane surface. They form four angles. Angles beside each other are adjacent angles. When they make a straight line, they add up to 180 degrees. Angles across the crossing are opposite angles, and they are equal. A clear justification of a mathematical statement is called a proof.
keyPoints: Intersecting lines meet at one point.
They form four angles.
Opposite angles are equal.
activities.explanation: You have met the main ideas for lines and angles.

activities.prompt: Match each description with its matching word or idea.
pairs: Adjacent angles on a straight line
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a key idea from this lesson. Check the shared word or idea.

activities.prompt: Angle a is 120 degrees. What must angle b be?
activities.explanation: The lesson states that angle b must be 60 degrees when angle a is 120 degrees.

activities.prompt: If angle b is 60 degrees, angle c must be 120 degrees.
activities.explanation: Yes. If angle b is 60 degrees, angle c must be 120 degrees.

activities.prompt: Two bus routes meet at one point and form four angles. If 6 marbles are placed in each angle, how many marbles are used?
activities.explanation: The intersecting routes form 4 angles, so the number of marbles is 4 * 6.

activities.prompt: Angle b is 120 degrees and angle d is opposite to it. What is angle d in degrees?
activities.explanation: Opposite angles b and d are equal, so d = b = 120 degrees.

activities.prompt: Angle a is 45 degrees and angle b is adjacent to it on a straight line. What is a+b in degrees?
activities.explanation: Adjacent angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees, so a+b = 45+(180-45) = 180 degrees.

activities.prompt: Angle a is 45 degrees and angle b is its adjacent angle on a straight line. Angles c and d are opposite a and b. What is a+b+c+d in degrees?
activities.explanation: a+b = 180 degrees and c+d = 180 degrees, so all four angles make 2*(180) = 360 degrees.

activities.prompt: Two bus routes cross each other. Angle x is 60 degrees and angle y is vertically opposite to it. What is angle y in degrees?
activities.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so y = x = 60 degrees.

activities.prompt: Use angle a as 120 degrees. Put these steps in order.
activities.explanation: First, angle a is 120 degrees. Next, angle b must be 60 degrees. Then, angle c must be 120 degrees.

activities.prompt: Angle b is 60 degrees and angle a is adjacent to it on a straight line. What is angle a in degrees?
activities.explanation: Angles a and b add to 180 degrees, so a = 180-60. In particular, when b is 60 degrees, a is 120 degrees.

lessons.title: 5.2 Perpendicular Lines and 5.3 Between Lines

activities.prompt: What can two lines do when they share the same plane?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Perpendicular and parallel lines
activities.body: When two intersecting lines form four equal angles, each is a right angle. Each angle is then 90 degrees. Perpendicular lines intersect each other. Segments FG and FH meet at endpoint F, where their angle is 115.3 degrees. Parallel lines stay apart on the same plane. They never meet, even when extended at both ends.
keyPoints: Perpendicular lines intersect each other.
Four equal angles each measure 90 degrees.
Parallel lines stay apart on the same plane.
activities.explanation: These are the main line relationships in this lesson.

activities.title: Lines that meet and lines that stay apart
activities.body: Perpendicular lines l and m intersect each other. Parallel lines stay apart on the same plane. Parallel lines never meet, even when extended at both ends. They must lie on the same plane. Artists often use parallel lines in artwork and shading.
keyPoints: Perpendicular lines l and m intersect.
Parallel lines lie on the same plane and do not meet.
Artists use parallel lines in artwork and shading.
activities.explanation: Perpendicular lines meet, while parallel lines stay apart.

activities.title: Perpendicular lines
activities.prompt: Which phrase describes perpendicular lines?
options: They stay apart on the same plane.
They do not meet when extended.
activities.explanation: Perpendicular lines intersect each other.

activities.title: Measure of equal angles
activities.prompt: Each of the four equal angles measures ______ degrees.
activities.hint: All four angles have the same measure.
activities.explanation: Each of the four equal angles measures 90 degrees.

activities.title: Match the line relationships
activities.prompt: Match each relationship with its matching detail.
pairs: stay apart on the same plane
do not meet even when extended
activities.explanation: The pairs show facts about intersecting, parallel, and joined lines.

activities.prompt: Two intersecting lines form four equal angles. Each equal angle measures 90 degrees. What is the measure of each angle in degrees?
activities.explanation: The four equal angles are right angles, so each one measures 90 degrees.

activities.prompt: Lines l and m are perpendicular and are 8 cm long. How many points do the two lines meet at?
activities.explanation: Perpendicular lines intersect at exactly 1 point.

activities.prompt: A drawing has 2 pairs of perpendicular lines. How many right angles are formed altogether?
activities.explanation: Each pair of perpendicular lines forms 4 right angles, so 2 * 4 = 8 right angles.

activities.prompt: Segment FG is 7 cm long and segment FH is 10 cm long. They meet at endpoint F. How many common endpoints do they have?
activities.explanation: Both segments meet at the same endpoint F, so they have 1 common endpoint.

activities.prompt: Segments FG and FH meet at F and form an angle of 115.3 degrees. A right angle measures 90 degrees. How many degrees must the angle be reduced to become a right angle?
activities.explanation: The angle must be reduced by 115.3 - 90 = 25.3 degrees.

activities.title: Order the angle steps
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
items: Two intersecting lines form four equal angles.
Each equal angle is a right angle.
activities.explanation: The equal angles are right angles, and each one measures 90 degrees.

activities.prompt: An artist draws 5 parallel lines on one sheet of paper. How many planes contain all the parallel lines?
activities.explanation: All the parallel lines lie on the same plane, so they are contained in 1 plane.

lessons.title: 5.4 Parallel and Perpendicular Lines in Paper Folding

activities.prompt: Can folding a square reveal hidden patterns of parallel and perpendicular lines?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Lines in a square and in paper folds
activities.body: Opposite edges of a square sheet are parallel. Adjacent edges are perpendicular. They meet at a point and form right angles. A first horizontal fold gives parallel lines. More horizontal folds give more parallel lines. A vertical fold line is perpendicular to horizontal fold lines. Arrow marks show parallel lines. A square angle mark shows perpendicular lines.
keyPoints: Opposite edges are parallel.
Adjacent edges are perpendicular.
Fold lines and marks show line relationships.
activities.explanation: Notice how folds and marks show relationships between lines.

activities.prompt: The first horizontal fold gives three parallel lines.
activities.explanation: Yes, the first horizontal fold gives three parallel lines.

activities.prompt: Which pair of edges meets at a right angle?
activities.explanation: Adjacent edges meet at a point and form right angles.

activities.prompt: Match each paper-folding clue to its meaning.
pairs: can create a line parallel to the diagonal
shows that a set of lines is parallel
activities.explanation: Each clue matches the line relationship shown in your book.

activities.prompt: A square wrapping paper has side 8 cm. What is the total length of one pair of opposite edges in cm?
activities.explanation: One pair of opposite edges has total length 2 * 8 cm.

activities.prompt: There are 3 square paper sheets. How many right angles are formed by their adjacent edges?
activities.explanation: Each square sheet has 4 right angles, so 3 sheets have 4 * 3 right angles.

activities.prompt: The first horizontal fold of a square sheet gives 3 parallel lines. If each line is 4 cm long, what is their total length in cm?
activities.explanation: The total length of the 3 parallel lines is 3 * 4 cm.

activities.prompt: Put these paper-folding results in the correct order.
items: First horizontal fold gives three parallel lines
After one more horizontal fold, there are five parallel lines
After one more horizontal fold, there are nine parallel lines
activities.explanation: Each extra horizontal fold adds more parallel lines in the pattern 2n + 1.

activities.prompt: A square sheet has one diagonal. If 2 diagonal fold lines are each parallel to that diagonal, how many fold-line-and-diagonal parallel pairs are there?
activities.explanation: Each of the 2 fold lines makes one parallel pair with the diagonal.

activities.prompt: One set of 2 parallel lines has one arrow mark on each line, and another set of 3 parallel lines has two arrow marks on each line. How many arrow marks are there?
activities.explanation: The first set needs 2 arrow marks and the second set needs 2 * 3 arrow marks, so the total is 2 + 2 * 3.

activities.prompt: One square angle mark is drawn at each of 4 meetings of perpendicular lines. How many square angle marks are drawn?
activities.explanation: One square angle mark is drawn at each meeting, so 4 meetings need 4 square angle marks.
