activities.prompt: There are 36 marbles divided equally among 6 children. What number of marbles per child is the multiplier that gives 36 when multiplied by 6?

activities.prompt: How can a tiny negative sign change the answer so dramatically?

activities.title: Division signs and grouped products
activities.body: When one integer is divided by another, signs guide the answer. A positive integer divided by a negative integer gives a negative quotient. A negative integer divided by a positive integer also gives a negative quotient. Dividing two negative integers gives the quotient of their positive values. Grouping multiplications differently does not change their product.
keyPoints: Dividing unlike signed integers gives a negative quotient.
Dividing two negative integers gives a positive quotient.
Different multiplication groups have the same product.
activities.explanation: These rules help you check the signs and groupings in your answers.

activities.title: Properties and Machine 1
activities.body: Multiplication can be grouped in different ways without changing its product. This is the associative property. With three or more integers, the product stays the same in any order. The distributive property also works for integers. Machine 1 adds the first two numbers. It then subtracts the third number.
keyPoints: Associative grouping keeps the product unchanged.
The product stays the same in any multiplication order.
Machine 1 adds the first two numbers, then subtracts the third.

Grouping multiplication always changes the product.
Grouped multiplications keep the same product.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing the Largest Square Tile

activities.prompt: Which square tile would be best for covering the whole room?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Find the largest tile
activities.body: The room has a breadth of 12 feet and a length of 16 feet. A tile must fit both sides exactly, so its side must be a common factor. The common factors are 1, 2 and 4. The HCF means the greatest of these common factors. It is 4. So Sameeksha should choose the 4 ft tile.
keyPoints: The tile must fit the breadth and length exactly.
The common factors are 1, 2 and 4.
The largest possible tile is 4 ft.
activities.explanation: The greatest common factor helps us choose the largest tile.

activities.title: A tile that fits
activities.prompt: A 2 ft tile can fit the breadth and length exactly.
activities.explanation: 2 is a common factor of 12 and 16, so this tile fits exactly.

activities.title: Find the HCF
activities.prompt: The HCF of 12 and 16 is ______.
activities.explanation: The greatest common factor of 12 and 16 is 4.

activities.title: Know the room
activities.prompt: What is the breadth of the room?
activities.explanation: The room has a breadth of 12 feet.

activities.prompt: A room is 16 ft broad. A square tile has side 1 ft and fits the breadth exactly. How many tiles fit across the breadth?
activities.explanation: Number of tiles across the breadth = 16 ÷ 1 = 16 tiles.

activities.prompt: A room is 12 ft long. A square tile has side 4 ft and fits the length exactly. How many tiles fit along the length?
activities.explanation: Number of tiles along the length = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 tiles.

activities.prompt: A room is 12 ft broad and 12 ft long. A square tile of side 4 ft fits both sides exactly. How many tiles are needed altogether?
activities.explanation: Tiles across the breadth = 12 ÷ 4. Tiles along the length = 12 ÷ 4. Total tiles = (12 ÷ 4) × (12 ÷ 4) = 9 tiles.

activities.prompt: A room is 12 ft broad. The number 3 is a factor of 12. How many equal parts of 3 ft make the breadth?
activities.explanation: Number of equal parts = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 parts.

activities.prompt: A room is 16 ft long. The number 4 is a factor of 16. How many equal parts of 4 ft make the length?
activities.explanation: Number of equal parts = 16 ÷ 4 = 4 parts.

activities.title: Order the tile sides
activities.prompt: Put the possible tile sides from smallest to largest.
activities.explanation: The order is 1 ft, 2 ft and 4 ft.

activities.prompt: A room is 12 ft broad and 16 ft long. A tile of side 4 ft fits both sides exactly. How many more tiles fit along the length than across the breadth?
activities.explanation: Tiles along the length = 16 ÷ 4. Tiles across the breadth = 12 ÷ 4. The difference is 1 tiles.

activities.title: Choosing a bag weight
activities.body: Lekhana has 84 kg of rice from one farm and 108 kg from another. Every bag must hold rice from only one farm. All bags must have the same whole-number weight. That weight must be a common factor of both amounts. The listed common factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. A 12 kg bag uses as few bags as possible. Prime factorisation is a method that can make this factor-finding process simpler.
keyPoints: Each bag holds rice from only one farm.
Every bag has the same whole-number weight.
The bag weight must be a common factor.
activities.explanation: Common factors help you choose one bag weight for both farms.

activities.prompt: Match each amount with its correct description.

activities.prompt: Put these common factors from smallest to largest.
activities.explanation: These listed common factors are already arranged from smallest to largest.

activities.prompt: Lekhana has 84 kg of rice from one farm. She fills each bag with 6 kg. How many bags does she make?
activities.explanation: For example, 84 ÷ 12 = 7, so 84 kg of rice makes 7 bags of 12 kg.

activities.prompt: Lekhana packs 84 kg and 108 kg of rice into separate bags of 12 kg each. How many bags does she use altogether?
activities.explanation: For 12 kg bags, she needs 84 ÷ 12 = 7 bags and 108 ÷ 12 = 9 bags, so she uses 7 + 9 = 16 bags.

activities.prompt: A shop receives 3 bags of rice, with 12 kg in each bag. How much rice is in all the bags?
activities.explanation: For example, 7 bags of 12 kg contain 7 × 12 = 84 kg of rice.

activities.prompt: How many 12 kg bags does Lekhana fill altogether?
activities.explanation: There are 7 bags for 84 kg and 9 bags for 108 kg. Altogether, she fills 16 bags.

activities.prompt: Using 6 kg bags needs more bags than using 12 kg bags.
activities.explanation: Six-kilogram bags need 14 and 18 bags from the farms. Together, they need 32 bags, which is more than 16.

activities.prompt: Lekhana packs each farm's rice into separate 6 kg bags. How many more bags does the 108 kg farm need than the 84 kg farm?
activities.explanation: For 12 kg bags, the difference is 9 − 7 = 2 bags.

activities.prompt: A rice amount has the prime factorisation 7**3 * 3**1. How many prime factors does it have when repeated factors are counted?
activities.explanation: For 2**2 * 3**1, there are 2 + 1 = 3 prime factors when repeats are counted.

activities.prompt: Two farm amounts are 2**2 * 7 * 3 kg and 2**2 * 7**3 kg, where 2, 7, and 3 are different prime numbers. What is their greatest common factor in kg?
activities.explanation: The shared prime parts are 2**2 and 7, so the greatest common factor is 2**2 * 7. For a = 2, b = 3, and c = 7, it is 12 kg.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Primes and Prime Factorisation

activities.prompt: What makes a number special, and how can we build it from smaller pieces?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding primes
activities.body: Primes are greater than 1. A prime has only 1 and itself as factors. The Sieve of Eratosthenes lists all primes. Any number is a product of primes. For 90, prime factorisation is 3 × 3 × 2 × 5. Reordering factors does not change their product. Different orders give the same prime factors. A prime factorises to itself. A composite is factorised until at least one factor is prime.
keyPoints: Primes are greater than 1 and have only 1 and themselves as factors.
The Sieve of Eratosthenes lists all primes.
activities.explanation: Prime factorisation writes any number as a product of primes.

activities.prompt: Match each number or idea with its matching result.
activities.explanation: The given products match the two numbers, and different orders keep the same prime factors.

activities.prompt: Which shows the prime factorisation of 105?
activities.explanation: 105 has the prime factors 3, 5 and 7.

activities.prompt: A shop has 2 boxes with 3 laddoos in each box. Both 2 and 3 are prime. How many laddoos are there?
activities.explanation: The total number of laddoos is 2 * 3 = 6 laddoos. These are prime factors.

activities.prompt: The prime factorisation of a number is 5 * 5. One prime factor is 5. What is the other prime factor?
activities.explanation: The two factors are 5 and 5. Therefore, the missing prime factor is 5.

activities.prompt: What is the prime factorisation of 7?
activities.explanation: The prime factorisation of a prime is the prime itself.

activities.prompt: There are 90 marbles. They are shared equally among 2 groups, where 2 is a prime factor of 90. How many marbles are in each group?
activities.explanation: Using 90 = 3 * 3 * 2 * 5, each group has 90 / 2 = 45 marbles.

activities.prompt: There are 105 laddoos. They are shared equally among 3 groups, where 3 is a prime factor of 105. How many laddoos are in each group?
activities.explanation: Using 105 = 3 * 5 * 7, each group has 105 / 3 = 35 laddoos.

activities.prompt: The Sieve of Eratosthenes lists 5, 2, and 2 as prime numbers. How many prime numbers are in the list?
activities.explanation: Each fraction equals 1, so the number of primes listed is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Factors and HCF Using Prime Factorisation

activities.prompt: Can we uncover every factor and the highest common factor using one clever method?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Factors and HCF
activities.body: Prime factorisation helps you find the factors of a number. For 225, the prime factorisation is 5 × 5 × 3 × 3. Every subpart gives a factor. The factors are 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 25, 45, 75 and 225. To find an HCF, take the minimum number of times each common prime appears. The largest common subpart also gives the HCF.
keyPoints: Prime factorisation can construct factors.
Every subpart gives a factor.
Minimum common prime counts give an HCF.
The factors of 225 are 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 25, 45, 75 and 225.
activities.explanation: These rules connect prime factorisation with factors and HCF.

activities.title: Checking Claims
activities.body: A conjecture is a claim made without proof or verification. A counterexample is an example that shows a conjecture is false. Use the complete factor list to check claims about 225. For example, 3 is a factor, but 5 is not a multiple of 3. So 5 can show that not every factor is a multiple of 3.
keyPoints: A conjecture lacks proof or verification.
A counterexample shows a conjecture is false.
Factor lists help you check claims.
activities.explanation: Examples help you check claims about factors.

activities.title: Find a Factor
activities.prompt: Which number is a factor of 225?
activities.explanation: The factor list includes 15, so it is a factor.

activities.title: Prime Subparts
activities.prompt: Every subpart of 5 × 5 × 3 × 3 gives a factor of 225.
activities.explanation: Each subpart of the prime factorisation gives a factor.

activities.title: Complete the Factorisation
activities.prompt: The prime factorisation of 225 is 5 × 5 × ______ × 3.
activities.hint: Look at the final two prime parts.
activities.explanation: This completes the listed prime factorisation.

activities.title: Match Products to Factors
activities.prompt: Match each prime product with its factor of 225.
activities.explanation: Each matched product is a subpart of 225. Each product also appears in the factor list.

activities.prompt: A box contains 7 × 11 × 7 × 2 marbles. How many marbles are in the box?
activities.explanation: Multiplying the prime factors gives the total: (7) × (11) × (7) × (2) = 1078 marbles.

activities.prompt: A bag contains 5 × 11 × 7 × 3 marbles. How many marbles are in the factor group 5 × 7?
activities.explanation: Every subpart of a prime factorisation gives a factor. Here the chosen subpart is (5) × (7) = 35 marbles.

activities.prompt: A marble count has 1 different prime factors. Each prime can be used 0, 1 or 2 times. How many different factors can be made?
activities.explanation: Each prime gives 3 choices, so the number of factors is (1) × 3 = 3. For 225, 2 × 3 × 3 = 9 factors.

activities.prompt: A child says, “Every box with more than 2 marbles can be split into equal groups of 29 marbles.” What number of marbles shows that the claim is false?
activities.explanation: The claim is a conjecture. The number 2 + 1 is a counterexample because it is more than 2 but cannot be split into equal groups of 29.

activities.prompt: Two lengths in cm have only common prime factors 13 and 29. The smaller counts of these primes are 1 and 3. What is their HCF in cm?
activities.explanation: Take the minimum number of times each common prime occurs: (13)^1 × (29)^3 = 317057 cm.

activities.prompt: The common factors of 112 cm and 84 cm include 1 cm, and no common factor is larger than 1 cm. What is their HCF in cm?
activities.explanation: The largest common subpart gives the HCF, so the HCF is 1 cm.

activities.prompt: What is the smallest length that two different people can both make?

activities.body: An LCM is the lowest of the common multiples. Anshu’s toran lengths are multiples of 6 cm. Guna’s toran lengths are multiples of 8 cm. Their shortest shared toran is 24 cm, so their least common multiple is 24 cm. To find an LCM, take the maximum number of occurrences of each prime.

24 cm is the shortest toran length shared by both children.
Use the maximum number of occurrences of each prime.

activities.title: LCMs and primes
activities.body: An LCM is the lowest of the common multiples. For 14 and 35, the LCM is 70. To find an LCM, take the maximum number of occurrences of each prime. The sweet shop gives free sweets every Monday. Kabamai next gets free sweets after 70 days, the same number as this LCM.
keyPoints: The LCM of 14 and 35 is 70.
Take the maximum number of occurrences of each prime.
Kabamai next gets free sweets after 70 days.
activities.explanation: Notice how 70 appears in two different examples.

activities.title: Is this true?
activities.prompt: The shortest toran that both children can stitch is 24 cm long.
activities.explanation: Yes. Their strips measure 6 cm and 8 cm, and 24 cm is their shortest shared length.

activities.title: Match each clue
activities.prompt: Match each clue with its correct detail.
activities.explanation: Great matching. You connected the strips, shared toran, and LCM.

activities.title: Find the shared toran
activities.prompt: Put the steps for finding the shared toran in order.
activities.explanation: You used a clear method. The lowest shared multiple is 24 cm.

activities.prompt: Anshu stitches 2 cloth strips, each 6 cm long. What is the total length of his toran in cm?

activities.prompt: Guna stitches 3 cloth strips, each 8 cm long. What is the total length of his toran in cm?

activities.prompt: A toran that both Anshu and Guna can stitch is 72 cm long. How many 6 cm strips does Anshu need?
activities.explanation: Divide the common toran length by the length of one Anshu strip: 72/6 strips.

activities.prompt: The sweet shop gives free sweets every Monday. Starting on Monday, how many Mondays come in 21 days?
activities.explanation: There are 7 days in a week, so divide the number of days by 7: 21/7 Mondays.

activities.title: Which pair gives 70?
activities.prompt: Kabamai next gets free sweets after 70 days. Which pair has an LCM of 70?
activities.explanation: The LCM of 14 and 35 is 70. It matches the 70-day wait.

activities.prompt: A common toran made with 14 cm and 35 cm strips is 70 cm long. How many 35 cm strips are needed?
activities.explanation: Divide the common toran length by the length of one 35 cm strip: 70/35 strips.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Patterns and Efficient Procedures

activities.prompt: Can you spot a quicker way to find common factors and multiples?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Finding patterns efficiently
activities.body: Patterns help us work efficiently. If one number factors another, their HCF is one of the given numbers. The other number is then a multiple of the first. Making a general statement is called generalisation. The number 5n is a multiple of n. So, the HCF of n and 5n is n. In the efficient procedure, divide both numbers by a common prime factor.
keyPoints: One given number can be the HCF.
Making a general statement is called generalisation.
Divide both numbers by a common prime factor.
activities.explanation: These patterns help you find HCFs efficiently.

activities.prompt: The HCF of 6 and 18 is 18.
activities.explanation: The HCF of 6 and 18 is 6.

activities.prompt: Which number is the HCF of 6 and 18?
activities.explanation: The HCF of 6 and 18 is 6.

activities.prompt: What is the HCF of n and 5n?
activities.explanation: Here, n is the HCF because 5n is a multiple of n.

activities.prompt: Match each pair with its HCF.
activities.explanation: Each pair uses the stated HCF.

activities.prompt: A bag has 3 marbles and another has 3×3 marbles. What is their HCF, in marbles?
activities.explanation: 3×3 is a multiple of 3, so the HCF is 3 marbles. For 3=6, the HCF of 6 and 18 is 6.

activities.prompt: One box has 5 marbles and another has 5×5 marbles. What is their HCF, in marbles?
activities.explanation: 5×5 is a multiple of 5, so their HCF is 5 marbles.

activities.prompt: The LCM of 3 cm and 8 cm is never greater than what number, in cm?
activities.explanation: The LCM is never greater than the product, so the upper bound is 3×8 cm.

activities.prompt: The two counts are 14×6 and 14×27. What is their HCF, in marbles?
activities.explanation: For every chosen 27, the HCF of 6 and 27 is 3. Therefore, the HCF is 14×3=42 marbles.

activities.prompt: Two lengths have HCF 2 cm and LCM 25 cm. What is the product of the two lengths, in cm²?
activities.explanation: The product of two numbers equals their HCF multiplied by their LCM, so the product is 2×25 cm².

activities.prompt: What is the LCM of 14 and 35?
activities.explanation: The LCM is the lowest of the common multiples. Here, it is 70.

activities.prompt: Put the HCF method steps in the correct order.
items: Write each number as a product of primes.
Find the common prime factors and their occurrences.
Take the minimum occurrence of each common prime.
activities.explanation: This method gives the HCF of 45 and 75 as 15.

lessons.title: Decimals: A Quick Recap

activities.prompt: How can one tiny dot change a whole number’s value?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Decimals Work
activities.body: Decimals extend the Indian place value system. In 27.53, you can see 2 tens, 7 ones, 5 tenths and 3 hundredths. A denominator is the lower number in a fraction. The game uses denominators 10, 100, 1000 and so on. Dividing by 10 moves the decimal point one place left.
keyPoints: Decimals use the Indian place value system.
27.53 has 2 tens, 7 ones, 5 tenths and 3 hundredths.
Dividing by 10 moves the decimal point left.
activities.explanation: Decimals help us show fractions smaller than one.

activities.title: Dividing with Larger Numbers
activities.body: Use larger divisors to place decimals carefully. Dividing 24 by 100 gives 0.24. Dividing 678 by 1000 gives 0.678. Dividing 12345 by 1000 gives 12.345. These examples use the decimal point to show each result. The game also uses fractions with denominators 10, 100, 1000 and so on.
keyPoints: Dividing 678 by 1000 gives 0.678.
Dividing 12345 by 1000 gives 12.345.
The game uses denominators 10, 100, 1000 and so on.
activities.explanation: Careful decimal placement gives the correct result.

activities.prompt: Which digit is in the tenths place of 27.53?
activities.explanation: The 5 is in the tenths place.

activities.prompt: Dividing by 10 moves the decimal point one place to the left.
activities.explanation: Yes, the decimal point moves one place left.

activities.prompt: Dividing 24 by 100 gives ______.
activities.hint: Divide, then place the decimal point correctly.
activities.explanation: Dividing 24 by 100 gives 0.24.

activities.prompt: Which calculation gives 0.678?
activities.explanation: Dividing 678 by 1000 gives 0.678.

activities.prompt: A number has 4 tenths and 8 hundredths. What is the number written in hundredths?
activities.explanation: Since 1 tenth = 10 hundredths, the number in hundredths is 10 * 4 + 8.

activities.prompt: A laddoo weighs 5 hundredths of a kilogram. What is its weight in kilograms?
activities.explanation: The denominator 100 means dividing by 100, so 5/100 gives the weight in kilograms.

activities.prompt: A bus ticket costs 5 tenths of a rupee, and 4 tickets are bought. What is the total cost in rupees?
activities.explanation: Multiply the number of tenths by the number of tickets and divide by 10 to find the total cost in rupees.

activities.prompt: A rope is 25 cm long. It is cut into 10 equal pieces. What is the length of each piece in cm?
activities.explanation: Dividing 25 by 10 moves the decimal point one place to the left and gives the length of each piece in cm.

activities.prompt: A shop has 40 grams of rice and packs it equally into 100 small packets. How many grams of rice are in each packet?
activities.explanation: Divide 40 grams by 100 to find the amount in each packet in grams.

activities.prompt: Each marble weighs 20 hundredths of a kilogram, and there are 4 marbles. What is their total weight in kilograms?
activities.explanation: Multiply the number of hundredths by the number of marbles and divide by 100 to find the total weight in kilograms.

lessons.title: Multiplying Decimals

activities.prompt: What clever trick makes multiplying decimals feel simple?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How to Multiply Decimals
activities.body: To multiply decimals, remove both decimal points and multiply the whole numbers. Then count the zeroes in the original denominators. Their sum tells you where to place the decimal point in the product. For example, 12.5 multiplied by 7.5 gives 93.75 km. This is because a car travels 12.5 km for each litre.
keyPoints: Remove each decimal point before multiplying.
Count the zeroes in both original denominators.
Use their sum to place the decimal point.
activities.explanation: The denominator zeroes help you place the decimal point correctly.

activities.prompt: One pen costs 9 rupees and 50 paisa.
activities.explanation: ₹9.5 means 9 rupees and 50 paisa. This helps you check the price.

activities.prompt: What is the cost of 5 pens?
activities.explanation: Multiply ₹9.5 by 5 to check this total. You get ₹47.5.

activities.prompt: Match each quantity or journey to its measurement.
activities.explanation: Each pair uses the matching measurement. Check each answer before moving on.

activities.prompt: A rectangle has sides 5.7 cm and 13.3 cm. Its area is ______ sq cm.
activities.explanation: Multiplying 5.7 by 13.3 gives 75.81. Remember the unit is square centimetres.

activities.prompt: One pen costs 15 rupees and 50 paisa. How many paisa does it cost?
activities.explanation: Each rupee has 100 paisa. Total paisa = 15*100 + 50 = 1550 paisa.

activities.prompt: One pen costs 15 rupees and 10 paisa. What is the cost of buying 5 pens in rupees?
activities.explanation: One pen costs (15*100 + 10)/100 rupees. For 5 pens, multiply and then convert back to rupees: (15*100 + 10)*5/100 = 75.5 rupees.

activities.prompt: A car travels 15.5 km for each litre of petrol. If it uses 1.1 litres, how far does it travel in km?
activities.explanation: Removing the decimal points gives (10*15+5) and (10*1+1). There are two decimal places in the product, so divide by 100.

activities.prompt: Ajay walks 827 metres each way between his school and home. In one week, he walks 6610 metres in total. How many round trips does he make?
activities.explanation: One round trip is 2*827 metres. Number of round trips = 6610/(2*827) = 3305/827.

activities.prompt: A car travels 15.3 km for each litre of petrol. If it uses 7.1 litres, how many hundredths of a kilometre are in the distance it travels?
activities.explanation: The numbers without decimal points are (10*15+3) and (10*7+1). Their product gives the distance measured in hundredths of a kilometre.

activities.prompt: A laddoo packet price in rupees has 2 digits after the decimal point. A marble box price in rupees has 2 digits after the decimal point. When the two prices are multiplied, how many zeroes are in the denominator of the product?
activities.explanation: The two original denominators have 2 and 2 zeroes. The product's denominator has 2+2 = 4 zeroes.

lessons.title: Comparing Decimal Products

activities.prompt: Can a product be smaller than both numbers being multiplied?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Products Can Change
activities.body: Multiplying decimals can make a product smaller, larger, or between the numbers. The product 2.25 × 8 is 18, greater than both numbers. The product 0.25 × 8 is 2, greater than 0.25 but less than 8. The product 0.25 × 0.8 is 0.2, less than both numbers. Decimals and fractions have similar multiplication relationships. A fraction product can also be less than both numbers.
keyPoints: A product may be greater than, between, or less than the numbers.
Decimals and fractions have similar multiplication relationships.
Compare each product with both original numbers.
activities.explanation: Comparing each product with both numbers helps you choose the right relationship.

activities.prompt: What is 2.25 multiplied by 8?
activities.explanation: Multiplying 2.25 by 8 gives 18.

activities.prompt: The product of 0.25 and 8 is greater than 0.25 but less than 8.
activities.explanation: The product is 2, so it lies above 0.25 and below 8.

activities.prompt: Multiplying 0.25 by 0.8 gives ______.
activities.hint: Compare the product with both numbers.
activities.explanation: Multiplying 0.25 by 0.8 gives 0.2.

activities.prompt: Match each multiplication with its product.
activities.explanation: Each expression matches the product shown beside it.

activities.prompt: A shop has 12 packets. Each packet has 0.25 kg of laddoos. What is the total weight in kg?
activities.explanation: Multiply 0.25 by 12. For 12 = 4, the total weight is 1 kg.

activities.prompt: A bus carries 16 boxes. Each box weighs 2.25 kg. What is the total weight in kg?
activities.explanation: Multiply 2.25 by 16. For 16 = 8, the total weight is 18 kg.

activities.prompt: A shop has 12 packets, each weighing 0.25 kg. How many more kg than 0.25 kg is the total weight?
activities.explanation: Find the total weight and subtract 0.25. For 12 = 8, the total is 2 kg, so the answer is 1.75 kg.

activities.prompt: A shop has 16 packets, each weighing 0.25 kg. How many fewer kg than 16 kg is the total weight?
activities.explanation: Subtract the total weight from 16. For 16 = 8, the total is 2 kg, so the answer is 6 kg.

activities.prompt: Each of 16 bags gets 0.25 kg of laddoos. The worker uses 0.8 of each amount. How many kg are used in all?
activities.explanation: First, 0.25 * 0.8 = 0.2. For 16 = 4, the total amount used is 0.8 kg.

lessons.title: Dividing Decimals

activities.prompt: How can we make dividing by decimals feel as easy as counting?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How to Divide Decimals
activities.body: A divisor is the number you divide by. The dividend is the number being divided. When dividing by 1, 10, 100 or 1000, move the decimal point left. Move it by the divisor's number of zeroes. So 3.9 m divided by 10 gives 0.39 m pieces. Divided by 100, it gives 0.039 m pieces. With a decimal divisor, multiply both the divisor and dividend by the same number.
keyPoints: 3.9 m divided by 10 gives 0.39 m pieces.
3.9 m divided by 100 gives 0.039 m pieces.
A decimal divisor needs matching multiplication.
activities.explanation: These rules help you keep each decimal in the right place.

activities.title: Equal Ribbon Pieces
activities.prompt: 3.9 m of ribbon is divided into 10 equal pieces. How long is each piece?
activities.explanation: Dividing 3.9 m by 10 moves the decimal point one place left.

activities.title: Move the Decimal Point
activities.prompt: Dividing by 100 moves the decimal point two places to the right.
activities.explanation: Dividing by 100 moves the decimal point two places left, not right.

activities.title: One Hundred Pieces
activities.prompt: Dividing 3.9 m into ______ equal pieces gives pieces of length 0.039 m.
activities.hint: Move the decimal point two places left.
activities.explanation: Dividing into 100 equal pieces gives 0.039 m for each piece.

activities.title: Match Divisions and Quotients
activities.prompt: Match each division with its quotient.
activities.explanation: Each pair uses the quotient shown for that division.

activities.prompt: A ribbon of 39 m is shared equally between 2 girls. How many m of ribbon does each girl get?
activities.explanation: Divide the ribbon length by 2. For 29 m, 29/2 = 14.5 m, which is 14 m and another 0.5 m.

activities.prompt: 1324 marbles are shared equally among 4 children. How many marbles does each child get?
activities.explanation: Regroup the hundreds before dividing. In 1324/4, regrouping makes 13 hundreds become 3 hundreds, and each part gets 3 hundreds.

activities.prompt: 1333 kg of sugar is shared equally among 4 bags. How many kg of sugar does each bag get?
activities.explanation: Divide the sugar mass by 4. For example, 1325/4 = 331.25 kg.

activities.prompt: There are 9.5 kg of sugar. It is shared equally among 1 bags. How many kg of sugar does each bag get?
activities.explanation: Divide 9.5 kg by the number of bags. For 4 bags, 9.5/4 = 2.375 kg per bag.

lessons.title: Quotients That Never End

activities.prompt: Why do some quotients keep going forever?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Quotients That Keep Going
activities.body: Some quotients keep going because their decimal forms never end. For 10 ÷ 3, there is no finite number of digits. With 1 ÷ 7, the remainders begin 1, 3, 2 and 6. The quotient's digits then repeat in a cycle. Cyclic means that digits move around in a repeating pattern. The number 142857 also cycles when multiplied from 1 to 6.
keyPoints: 10 ÷ 3 cannot have a finite number of digits.
The remainders for 1 ÷ 7 start with 1, 3, 2 and 6.
Cyclic numbers have digits that move around in a repeating pattern.
activities.explanation: These examples show how repeated remainders can create cycling digits.

activities.title: An Unsolved Idea and Bigger Quotients
activities.body: Emil Artin conjectured that there must be infinitely many cyclic numbers. A conjecture is an idea proposed for proof. His conjecture remains unsolved. Dividing can also make a quotient smaller or larger than the dividend. Whole-number division gives a smaller quotient, while 128 ÷ 0.4 gives 320.
keyPoints: Artin conjectured that infinitely many cyclic numbers must exist.
His conjecture remains unsolved.
128 ÷ 0.4 gives a quotient greater than the dividend.
activities.explanation: Cyclic numbers remain mysterious, but division can give different-sized quotients.

activities.prompt: The decimal form of 10 ÷ 3 has a finite number of digits.
activities.explanation: The decimal form of 10 ÷ 3 cannot have a finite number of digits.

activities.prompt: When 1 is divided by 7, the first remainders are 1, 3, 2 and ______.
activities.hint: This remainder completes the starting sequence.
activities.explanation: The remainders start with 1, 3, 2 and 6.

activities.prompt: Match each remainder position with its starting remainder.
activities.explanation: The remainders for 1 ÷ 7 start with 1, 3, 2 and 6.

activities.prompt: There are 12 marbles shared equally among 3 children. How many marbles does each child get?
activities.explanation: Marbles in each child's group = total marbles ÷ number of groups = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 marbles.

activities.prompt: There are 60 laddoos packed equally into boxes, with 2 laddoos in each box. How many boxes are needed?
activities.explanation: Number of boxes = total laddoos ÷ laddoos in each box = 60 ÷ 2 = 30 boxes.

activities.prompt: A bus travels 120 km in 5 tenths of an hour. What is its speed in km per hour?
activities.explanation: Speed in km per hour = distance in km ÷ time in hours = 120 ÷ (5 ÷ 10) = 240 km per hour.

activities.prompt: Put the starting remainders in the order shown when 1 is divided by 7.
activities.explanation: The starting remainders are 1, 3, 2 and 6.

activities.prompt: 10 marbles are divided equally among 3 children. What is the quotient in marbles?
activities.explanation: The quotient is 10 ÷ 3. For example, 10 ÷ 3 = 3.333..., so the decimal quotient has no last digit.

activities.prompt: A number card shows the product of 142857 and 2. What number is on the card?
activities.explanation: The number on the card is 142857 × 2. These products have the same digits arranged in different cyclic orders.

lessons.title: Look Before You Leap

activities.prompt: Why do we add an extra day every four years?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why Calendar Years Change
activities.body: A revolution is one trip around the Sun. A calendar year has 365 days for convenience. The Earth needs 0.2422 more days after 365 days. A leap year adds one extra day every fourth year. Earlier rules gave too many days. Calendar makers stopped adding a day in every hundredth year. They made every 400th year a leap year.
keyPoints: A revolution is one trip around the Sun.
A calendar year uses 365 days.
Leap-year rules change with long periods.
activities.explanation: These ideas explain why calendar years need special rules.

activities.title: Days Still Needed
activities.prompt: After 365 days, the Earth still needs ______ more days.
activities.explanation: The Earth still needs 0.2422 days after 365 days.

activities.title: Match the Calendar Facts
activities.prompt: Match each calendar fact with its correct value.
pairs: Add one day every fourth year
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a calendar rule with the matching time.

activities.prompt: One bus card stands for one calendar year of 365 days. If 10 bus cards are used, how many days do they represent?
activities.explanation: Calendar days = 365 * years. For years = 1, the bus cards represent 365 days.

activities.prompt: One marble stands for the extra day in a leap year. If every fourth year is a leap year for 4 years, how many marbles are needed?
activities.explanation: Extra leap days = years / 4. For years = 4, the marbles represent 1 extra day.

activities.prompt: In each group of 100 years, 24 years are leap years and 76 years have 365 days. How many leap years are there in 5 such groups?
activities.explanation: Number of leap years = 24 * groups. For groups = 10, there are 240 leap years.

activities.title: The Difference After 1000 Years
activities.prompt: What difference remained after 1000 years under the earlier scheme?
activities.explanation: The earlier scheme left a difference of 2.2 days after 1000 years.

activities.title: The 400th-Year Rule
activities.prompt: What happened after 1000 years when every 400th year was a leap year?
activities.explanation: The calendar became slightly shorter than the actual time.

activities.prompt: In each group of 100 years, the calendar has 36524 days while Earth takes 36524.22 days. For 10 groups, what is the difference in days?
activities.explanation: Difference in days = (36524.22 - 36524) * groups. For groups = 10, the difference is 2.2 days.

activities.prompt: Every fourth year is a leap year, every hundredth year is not, but every four-hundredth year is. How many days are in 1200 years of this calendar?
activities.explanation: Calendar days = 365 * years + years / 4 - years / 100 + years / 400. For years = 400, the calendar has 146097 days.

lessons.title: Questions and Statistical Statements

activities.prompt: How can data help us make better guesses?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Statistical Ideas
activities.body: Statistics means studying data by collecting, sorting, examining, explaining and showing it. Statistical questions can be answered by collecting data. Statistical statements tell us about patterns, amounts or predictions. They may use numbers, proportions, probabilities or predictions. Proportions show parts of a group, and probabilities show chances. Studying data and graphs helps us draw suitable conclusions. Guesses from patterns can sometimes be wrong.
keyPoints: Statistics helps us study data from collection to presentation
Statistical questions can be answered by collecting data
Statistical statements can give information or make predictions
activities.explanation: These ideas help you study data and make careful conclusions.

activities.prompt: Statistical thinking helps us make guesses from patterns in information.
activities.explanation: Patterns give clues for making guesses, but such guesses may sometimes be wrong.

activities.prompt: Match each action to the idea it supports.
activities.explanation: Each action matches an important use of data from the lesson.

activities.prompt: A statistical question can be answered by ______ data.
activities.hint: Choose the action that brings in information.
activities.explanation: Collecting data gives us information that we can study to answer a statistical question.

activities.prompt: A survey of Grade 7 students found 18 students in Class 7A and 22 students in Class 7B. How many students were surveyed in total?
activities.explanation: Total students surveyed = 18 + 22 = 40.

activities.prompt: There are 5 boxes with 10 laddoos in each box. How many laddoos are there in all?
activities.explanation: Multiply the number of boxes by the number of laddoos in each box: 5 * 10 = 50 laddoos.

activities.prompt: On Day 1, 8 buses arrive, and 2 more buses arrive each day. How many buses arrive on Day 3?
activities.explanation: The number on Day 3 is 8 + (3 - 1) * 2 = 12 buses.

activities.prompt: The price of 1 kg of onions was 12 rupees earlier and is 25 rupees now. By how many rupees did the price increase?
activities.explanation: Subtract the earlier price from the present price: 25 - 12 = 13 rupees.

activities.prompt: Onions cost 15 rupees per kg in Yahapur and 8 rupees per kg in Wahapur. How many rupees more per kg do they cost in Yahapur?
activities.explanation: Subtract the Wahapur price from the Yahapur price: 15 - 8 = 7 rupees per kg.

activities.title: The Steps in Statistics
activities.prompt: Put the parts of statistics in the order given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Statistics follows this sequence. Each step helps us study data properly.

activities.prompt: A bag has 3 red marbles, 3 green marbles and 3 yellow marbles. What is the probability of picking a red marble, as a fraction?
activities.explanation: Total marbles = 3 + 3 + 3. The probability of a red marble is red marbles divided by all marbles: 1/3.

lessons.title: Finding a Representative Value

activities.prompt: What number can tell us what a group of values is usually like?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is an average?
activities.body: A representative value helps you compare groups fairly. It balances the high and low values in a group. The average is also called the mean. To find the mean, divide the total of all values by the number of values. A total may not be fair when groups have different sizes.
keyPoints: A representative value balances high and low values.
The average is also called the mean.
Divide the total by the number of values.
activities.explanation: The average gives a fair share and balances high and low values.

activities.title: Shubman's average
activities.prompt: What was Shubman's average in the second series?
activities.explanation: Shubman's average was 21 runs per match in the second series.

activities.title: Two names for the same idea
activities.prompt: The arithmetic mean is another name for the average.
activities.explanation: Yes! The average is also called the arithmetic mean or mean.

activities.title: Name the average
activities.prompt: The average is also called the arithmetic ______.
activities.hint: This word has fewer letters than 'average'.
activities.explanation: The arithmetic mean is another name for the average.

activities.title: The higher average
activities.prompt: Whose average was higher in the second series?
activities.explanation: Yashasvi's average was 24 runs per match in the second series.

activities.prompt: Two equal-sized groups have 18 marbles and 21 marbles. How many more marbles does the second group have?
activities.explanation: Because the groups have the same size, their totals can be compared. The correct formula is t2 - t1, which gives the extra number of marbles in the second group.

activities.prompt: Shubman's average is 21 runs per match, and Yashasvi's average is 24 runs per match. How many more runs per match does Yashasvi have?
activities.explanation: Yashasvi has the higher average. The correct formula is y - s, which gives the difference in runs per match.

activities.prompt: One group has 2 marbles, and another has 18 marbles. What representative number balances the low and high values?
activities.explanation: Add the low and high values and divide by 2. Using 2 and 18, the representative value is 10 marbles.

activities.prompt: Group A has 2 children and 80 laddoos. Group B has 3 children and 30 laddoos. How many more laddoos per child does Group A get?
activities.explanation: Find each group's fair share by dividing its total by its number of children. Then subtract Group B's share from Group A's share to find the difference in laddoos per child.

lessons.title: Medians and Outliers

activities.prompt: How can one middle height reveal what an average misses?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the median
activities.body: The median is the middle number after you sort the data. For an even number of values, average the two middle numbers. An outlier differs greatly from the other values. Poovizhi’s sorted heights were 118, 165, 170, 173 and 175 cm. Their median was 170 cm. The outliers did not greatly affect the median.
keyPoints: Sort the data before finding the median.
The median is the middle number.
Outliers differ greatly from the other values.
activities.explanation: A median shows the middle of sorted data.

activities.title: Choose the median height

activities.explanation: The middle number in the sorted heights was 170 cm.

activities.title: Fill the median

activities.explanation: The middle number in the sorted heights was 170.

activities.title: An even number of values

Sort and average the two middle numbers
Choose the greatest and smallest values
Choose any number from the data

activities.prompt: Four sorted heights are 154, 160, 168 and 178 cm. What is the median height in cm?

activities.prompt: Five family heights were recorded as 175, 166, 177, 119 and 170 cm. Sort them and give the median height in cm.

activities.prompt: Poovizhi’s family average height is 159 cm and Yaangba’s family average height is 168 cm. Which calculation gives the lower average height in cm?

activities.explanation: Divide the total height by the number of people: 805 / 5 cm.

activities.prompt: Poovizhi’s sorted heights are 119, 166, 172, 174 and 175 cm. Which calculation gives the height in cm that represents the family heights better?

activities.prompt: What can we discover by comparing averages, medians, and the shortest and tallest heights?

activities.title: The Ends and Middle of Data
activities.body: The minimum is the smallest value. The maximum is the largest value. The mean is the average. The median is the middle value. An outlier is an unusual value. Balanced data usually has a mean close to its median. A low outlier pulls the mean down. A high outlier pulls the mean up.
keyPoints: The minimum and maximum are the two extremes.
The mean is the average, and the median is the middle value.
A low outlier pulls the mean down.
A high outlier pulls the mean up.
activities.explanation: These words help you describe the ends and middle of data.

activities.title: What the Class Heights Show
activities.body: In this class, the girls’ heights ranged from 136 cm to 156 cm. The tallest and shortest students were boys. The boys’ average height was below the whole-class average. The girls had a greater average height than the boys. These facts do not mean that every girl was taller than every boy.
keyPoints: The girls’ heights ranged from 136 cm to 156 cm.
The tallest and shortest students were boys.
A group’s average does not describe every member.
activities.explanation: These details show how averages and extremes can differ within one class.

activities.prompt: The minimum and maximum are the two extremes of data.
activities.explanation: The minimum and maximum are the two extreme values in data.

activities.prompt: What was the girls’ minimum height?
activities.explanation: The girls’ heights ranged from 136 cm, so 136 cm was the minimum.

activities.prompt: For the boys, the mean was ______ the median.
activities.explanation: The boys’ mean was below their median.

activities.prompt: The shortest height in a group is 144 cm and the tallest height is 156 cm. What is the range of the heights in cm?
activities.explanation: Range = tallest height - shortest height = 156 - 144 = 12 cm.

activities.prompt: Three girls have heights 136 cm, 148 cm, and 150 cm. What is their average height in cm?
The whole-class average height is 154 cm, and the boys’ average height is 145 cm. How many cm lower is the boys’ average than the whole-class average?
activities.explanation: Difference = whole-class average - boys’ average = 154 - 145 = 9 cm.

activities.prompt: The girls’ average height is 154 cm, and the boys’ average height is 144 cm. How many cm greater is the girls’ average?
activities.explanation: Difference = girls’ average - boys’ average = 154 - 144 = 10 cm.

activities.prompt: Put the high-outlier effect in order.
items: The mean moves towards the higher end
activities.explanation: A high outlier pulls the mean towards the higher end.

activities.prompt: For the boys, the mean height is 142 cm and the median height is 146 cm. How many cm is the median above the mean?
activities.explanation: Difference = median - mean = 146 - 142 = 4 cm. The mean is below the median.

activities.prompt: For the girls, the mean height is 148 cm and the median height is 152 cm. How many cm is the median above the mean?
activities.explanation: Difference = median - mean = 152 - 148 = 4 cm. The mean is below the median.

Paired bars can form a clustered column graph.
Two bars in each cluster make a double column graph.
Markings on the vertical line help estimate differences.

Opposite daylight patterns came from opposite hemispheres.
Paired bar heights show where onions were costlier.
Vertical markings help estimate differences.

lessons.title: Eyes and the Perpendicular Bisector

activities.prompt: How can we make an eye perfectly symmetrical with a simple line?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Building a Symmetrical Eye
activities.body: An eye drawing uses matching upper and lower arcs. Both arcs must have the same radius. Draw arcs above and below XY from X and Y. Their intersections give centres A and B. The line AB passes through the midpoint of XY and crosses it at a right angle. A perpendicular bisector divides a line into two equal parts and is perpendicular to it.
keyPoints: The upper and lower arcs have the same radius.
The arc intersections give centres A and B.
AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.
activities.explanation: Matching arcs and equal distances help you draw a symmetrical eye.

activities.title: Finding the Perpendicular Bisector
activities.body: First, note the line XY. Draw arcs above and below it from both X and Y. The intersections give centres A and B. The line AB passes through the midpoint of XY and is perpendicular to XY. Bisection means dividing a geometrical object into two identical parts. Therefore, AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.
keyPoints: Draw arcs from both X and Y.
The arc intersections give centres A and B.
AB bisects XY and is perpendicular to it.
activities.explanation: The arc intersections help you locate the perpendicular bisector.

activities.title: Matching the Arcs
activities.prompt: What must the upper and lower arcs have?
activities.explanation: The upper and lower arcs must have the same radius.

activities.title: The Supporting Line
activities.prompt: Line XY remains in the final eye drawing.
activities.explanation: Line XY supports the eye drawing, but it is not part of the final figure.

activities.title: Important Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct description.
pairs: Dividing a geometrical object into two identical parts
activities.explanation: Each description matches an important idea from the lesson.

activities.prompt: A pupil draws 4 curved eye arcs and one supporting line XY, which is not part of the final drawing. How many curved arcs are in the final drawing?
activities.explanation: The supporting line XY is not part of the final drawing, so only the 4 curved arcs are counted.

activities.prompt: The line XY is 10 cm long and O is its midpoint. How many cm long is XO?
activities.explanation: The midpoint divides XY into two equal parts, so XO is half of 10 cm.

activities.prompt: The distances AX and AY are both 4 cm. What is the sum of AX and AY in cm?
activities.explanation: AX and AY are equal, so their sum is 4 + 4 cm.

activities.title: Constructing the Perpendicular Bisector
activities.prompt: Put the construction steps in order.
items: Draw arcs above and below XY from X and Y
Identify centres A and B at the arc intersections
Draw line AB through midpoint O
Check that AB is perpendicular to XY
activities.explanation: The arcs locate the centres, and AB forms the perpendicular bisector.

activities.prompt: The distances AX, AY, BX and BY are all 3 cm. What is the sum of all four distances in cm?
activities.explanation: All four distances equal 3 cm, so their sum is four times 3 cm.

activities.prompt: For 4 eye drawings, arcs above and below XY meet at two centres, A and B, in each drawing. How many centres are marked altogether?
activities.explanation: Each eye drawing has two centres, so 4 drawings have 4 + 4 centres.

activities.prompt: At O, AB is perpendicular to XY, making 3 right angles. What is the sum of these angles in degrees?
activities.explanation: Each right angle measures 90 degrees, so the sum of 3 right angles is 3 × 90 degrees.

lessons.title: Right Angles and Ancient Rope Methods

activities.prompt: Could an ancient rope reveal where a hidden midpoint lies?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Constructing a Perpendicular Bisector
activities.body: A perpendicular bisector is a line through the midpoint of XY and perpendicular to XY. To construct one, draw two long arcs above XY. Let their meeting point be A. Draw equal-radius arcs below XY, meeting at B. Join A to B. This line is the required perpendicular bisector. You can do this with an unmarked ruler and compass.
keyPoints: A perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint of XY.
A and B are the arc meeting points above and below XY.
AB is the required perpendicular bisector.
activities.explanation: These steps use equal-distance points to make a perpendicular bisector.

activities.title: Midpoints and Ancient Rope Methods
activities.body: When O is already the midpoint of XY, the perpendicular bisector passes through O and is perpendicular to XY. Only one pair of intersecting arcs is needed. Ancient mathematicians from different civilizations knew exact construction methods. The Śulba-Sūtras are geometric texts from the Vedic period. They used a compass made from a rope, and a folded rope can find and mark its midpoint.
keyPoints: One pair of arcs is enough when O is the midpoint.
Different civilizations knew exact construction methods.
The Śulba-Sūtras used a rope-made compass.
activities.explanation: Ancient methods used geometry, intersecting arcs and folded ropes.

activities.prompt: What do two equal-distance points above and below XY determine?
activities.explanation: These equal-distance points are A and B. Their line is the perpendicular bisector.

activities.prompt: A folded rope can find the midpoint but cannot mark it.
activities.explanation: A folded rope can find and mark its midpoint. This useful method works beautifully.

activities.prompt: Match each label with its correct role.
pairs: the upper meeting point of two long arcs
the lower meeting point of two long arcs
activities.explanation: A and B come from the arcs. O marks the midpoint, and AB joins the arc points.

activities.prompt: One unmarked ruler costs 12 rupees and one compass costs 18 rupees. What is the total cost in rupees?
activities.explanation: Total cost = 12 + 18 = 30 rupees.

activities.prompt: Equal groups of marbles are placed at X and Y, with O halfway between them. If each group has 8 marbles, how many marbles are there from X to Y?
activities.explanation: The number of marbles = 8 + 8 = 16.

activities.prompt: A 12 cm rope is folded to mark its midpoint. How many cm from one end is the midpoint?
activities.explanation: The midpoint is 12 / 2 = 6 cm from one end.

activities.prompt: At a known midpoint O, one upper and one lower long arc are drawn with radius 3 cm. What is the sum of their radii in cm?
activities.explanation: The sum of the two radii = 3 + 3 = 6 cm.

activities.prompt: Point A is 6 cm above XY and point B is 3 cm below XY on the constructed perpendicular bisector AB. What is the length AB in cm?
activities.explanation: The length AB = 6 + 3 = 9 cm.

activities.prompt: Put these construction steps in the correct order.
items: Construct two long arcs above XY
Construct two long arcs below XY using the same radius
activities.explanation: The arcs meet at A above XY and at B below XY. Joining them gives AB.

activities.prompt: A bus route is drawn as the perpendicular bisector through midpoint O of road XY. Stop P is 4 cm from O along the route. How far is P from road XY in cm?
activities.explanation: Since OP is perpendicular to XY, the distance from P to XY = 4 cm.

lessons.title: Bisecting and Copying Angles

activities.prompt: Can you make a perfect half-angle and copy it with just an arc?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How angles can be bisected and copied
activities.body: To bisect an angle, mark A and B so OA equals OB. Draw arcs from A and B using the same radius. The meeting point of the equal-radius arcs is C. SSS shows triangles OBC and OAC are congruent. To copy an angle, draw a same-radius arc from X. Transfer the measured length from Z to obtain Y. Congruent copied triangles make the copied angles equal.
keyPoints: Equal-radius arcs meet at C.
SSS proves the two triangles are congruent.
Congruent copied triangles give equal copied angles.
activities.explanation: Equal lengths and matching arcs help you construct and copy angles.

activities.title: Equal parts of a full turn
activities.prompt: What is the size of every angle when 360° has eight equal parts?
activities.explanation: Dividing 360° into eight equal parts gives 45° for every design angle.

activities.prompt: Arcs from A and B use the same radius.
activities.explanation: Draw arcs from A and B using the same radius.

activities.title: Match the construction clues
activities.prompt: Match each construction clue with its result.
activities.explanation: These pairs show which equal lengths and meeting points guide the construction.

activities.title: Order the bisecting steps
activities.prompt: Put the angle-bisecting steps in order.
items: Mark A and B so OA equals OB.
Draw equal-radius arcs from A and B.
The equal-radius arcs meet at C.
Prove triangles OBC and OAC congruent by SSS.
activities.explanation: Equal sides come first, then the arcs, and finally the congruence proof.

activities.prompt: A round design has 4 equal parts around its center. What angle, in degrees, does each part make?
activities.explanation: The full angle is 360 degrees. For n = 8, 360/8 = 45 degrees.

activities.prompt: Two congruent triangles are used to bisect an angle of 60 degrees. What is the measure of each half in degrees?
activities.explanation: Bisecting means dividing the angle into two equal parts. For a = 40, 40/2 = 20 degrees.

activities.prompt: OA and OB each measure 6 cm, and AC and BC each measure 5 cm. What is the total length of OA, OB, AC, and BC in cm?
activities.explanation: There are two sides of length r and two sides of length c. For r = 3 and c = 2, 2*3+2*2 = 10 cm.

activities.prompt: For congruent triangles OBC and OAC, OA and OB measure 5 cm each, AC and BC measure 2 cm each, and the shared side OC measures 5 cm. What is the total length of the three matching sides, counting OC once, in cm?
activities.explanation: The matching sides are OA and OB, AC and BC, and the shared side OC. For r = 3, a = 2, and c = 3, 2*3+2*2+3 = 13 cm.

activities.prompt: When copying an angle, an arc of radius 6 cm is drawn from X. The copied arc drawn from Y uses the same radius. What is the radius of the copied arc in cm?
activities.explanation: The two arcs use the same radius. For r = 3, the copied arc has radius 3 cm.

activities.prompt: The length XZ on an angle is 4 cm. This length is transferred to obtain YZ. What is the length YZ in cm?
activities.explanation: The transferred length stays the same. For d = 4, YZ = 4 cm.

lessons.title: Parallel Lines and Arch Designs

activities.prompt: Can you build a beautiful arch using only straight lines and gentle curves?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Lines and arches
activities.body: A transversal is the line l that meets the given line and the parallel line. The parallel line must make the same corresponding angle as the given line. For construction, draw equal-radius arcs from points A and B. Transfer the length CD to the arc from F. This makes a line parallel to the given line. A symmetrical arch needs AB equal to CD. Its two end angles must match.
keyPoints: Line l is the transversal.
The parallel line uses the same corresponding angle.
Equal-radius arcs help construct the parallel line.
AB equals CD and the end angles match.
activities.explanation: These rules help you construct parallel lines and symmetrical arches.

activities.title: Designing a symmetrical arch
activities.body: A symmetrical arch needs AB equal to CD. The two end angles must match. Construct equal angles at A and D. Mark B and C so AB equals CD. For the arch's arcs, change their radii to improve its appearance. A pointed arch has two supporting lines. Each is a line segment. Both supporting segments have equal length.
keyPoints: AB and CD must have equal lengths.
Construct equal angles at A and D.
Adjust arc radii to improve appearance.
Both supporting line segments have equal length.
activities.explanation: Use these rules when marking and shaping a symmetrical arch.

activities.prompt: Which line serves as a transversal in the construction?
activities.explanation: Line l serves as the transversal to both lines.

activities.prompt: The parallel line must make a different corresponding angle from the given line.
activities.explanation: It must make the same corresponding angle as the given line.

activities.prompt: Match each construction clue to its detail.
activities.explanation: Draw equal-radius arcs from A and B. Transfer CD to the arc from F. The procedure constructs a parallel line.

activities.prompt: A bus route l crosses two parallel road lines as a transversal. If the angle on the first road line is 90°, what is the corresponding angle on the other road line in degrees?
activities.explanation: Parallel lines make equal corresponding angles, so the answer is 90°.

activities.prompt: Arcs of equal radius are drawn from A and B. If each radius is 3 cm, what is the radius of each arc in cm?
activities.explanation: The arcs have equal radii, so each radius is 3 cm.

activities.prompt: A length of 4 cm from C to D is transferred to an arc from F. What is the length from F to the marked point in cm?
activities.explanation: Transferring CD preserves its length, so the new length is 4 cm.

activities.prompt: For a symmetrical arch, mark B and C so that AB equals CD. If CD is 6 cm, what is AB in cm?
activities.explanation: A symmetrical arch has AB equal to CD, so AB is 6 cm.

activities.prompt: Put the parallel-line construction steps in order.
items: Draw equal-radius arcs from A and B.
Transfer the length CD to the arc from F.

activities.explanation: An equation is a balance: both sides must be equal.

activities.title: Making a Weighing Puzzle Easier

The hint asks you to remove objects until only sacks remain on one plate.
Three bread slices balance two eggs.

activities.prompt: On a weighing scale, 3 laddoos on one plate balance 3 laddoos on the other. If each laddoo weighs 1 unit, what is the total weight of all the laddoos in units?

activities.prompt: 6 equal sacks balance a total weight of 6 units. What is the weight of one sack in units?
activities.explanation: The equal sacks share the 6 units equally, so one sack weighs 6/n units.

activities.prompt: There are 15 marbles on each plate of a balanced scale. If 3 marbles are removed from each plate, how many marbles remain on each plate?
activities.explanation: Removing r marbles from n leaves n-r marbles on each plate.

activities.prompt: Unknown weights 6 units and 3 units are placed together on one plate. What is their combined weight in units?
activities.explanation: Placing the unknown weights together on one plate means adding their weights, so the result is x+y units.

activities.prompt: There are 7 sacks on one plate and 4 sacks on the other. Remove 4 sacks from each plate so that sacks remain on only one plate. How many sacks remain on that plate?
activities.explanation: After removing m sacks from each plate, the first plate has n-m sacks and the second plate has no sacks.

activities.explanation: Removing equal weights from both plates keeps the scale balanced.

activities.title: Patterns, Equations and Their Parts
activities.body: First arrangement: 3 sticks. Second arrangement: 5 sticks. At position n, the pattern uses 2n + 1 sticks. Jasmine wants exactly 99 sticks. An equation states that two algebraic expressions are equal. The word equation names this statement. LHS means Left Hand Side; RHS means Right Hand Side. Solving finds the letter-numbers for which an equation holds.
keyPoints: First arrangement: 3 sticks; second: 5 sticks.
Position n uses 2n + 1 sticks.
LHS and RHS are the two sides of an equation.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you find patterns and solve equations.

activities.title: First Arrangement
activities.prompt: How many sticks does the first matchstick arrangement use?
activities.explanation: The first matchstick arrangement uses 3 sticks.

activities.title: Second Arrangement
activities.prompt: The second matchstick arrangement uses 5 sticks.

activities.title: Meaning of an Equation
activities.prompt: An equation is a statement of ______ between two algebraic expressions.

activities.title: Meaning of RHS

activities.title: Matchstick Rule

activities.title: Match the Names

activities.title: Jasmine's Arrangement

activities.title: Parts of an Equation

activities.prompt: The LHS is 2*n+1 and the RHS is n+3. At which position n is LHS = RHS?
activities.explanation: Making the two sides equal gives 2*n+1=n+b, so n=b-1. For b=4, the position is 3.

lessons.title: Trying Values by Trial and Error

activities.prompt: Ready to discover which number makes the equation balance?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Trying Values
activities.body: Trial and error means replacing the letter-number with different values and checking the results. For 2n + 1 = 99, n = 49 gives 99, so it is the solution. Trying n = 5 gives 11, and n = 40 gives 81. This method can be inefficient. Another example is 5x – 4 = 7. The same operation on both sides keeps their equality. Inverse pairs are addition and subtraction, and multiplication and division.
keyPoints: Try different values and check them.
The solution of 2n + 1 = 99 is n = 49.
Trial and error can be inefficient.
Inverse operations can undo work.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows how checking values can reveal a solution.

activities.title: Balance the scale

tasks.then: The left side is too light: 7 is less than 11.

tasks.say: Find the x that balances it.
tasks.then: 2 x 4 + 3 = 11, so both sides are equal.

activities.takeaway: An equation is a balance: both sides must be equal.
activities.explanation: An equation is a balance: both sides must be equal.

activities.title: Keeping Equality
activities.body: When you perform the same operation on both sides of an equation, their equality does not change. Addition and subtraction are inverse operations. Multiplication and division are inverse operations. This helps you undo work when checking equations. You can use trial and error for 5x – 4 = 7 too, although the method may be inefficient.
keyPoints: Same operations keep both sides equal.
Addition undoes subtraction.
Subtraction undoes addition.
Multiplication and division undo each other.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you keep an equation balanced while checking values.

activities.title: Check a Value
activities.prompt: Trying n = 5 gives a left-hand value of 11.
activities.explanation: Yes, the left-hand value is 11 when n = 5.

activities.title: Find the Checked Value
activities.prompt: Trying n = 40 gives a left-hand value of ______.
activities.explanation: The left-hand value is 81 when n = 40.

activities.title: Find the Solution
activities.prompt: What is the solution of 2n + 1 = 99?
activities.explanation: Trying n = 49 gives a left-hand value of 99.

activities.title: Match Values with Results
activities.prompt: Match each value of n with its left-hand value for 2n + 1 = 99.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows the result after replacing n with that value.

activities.prompt: A shopkeeper puts 40 laddoos in each of 2 boxes and has 1 extra laddoo. How many laddoos are there in all?
activities.explanation: The total is 2 x 40 + 1 = 81 laddoos. Thus n = 5 gives 11, n = 40 gives 81, and n = 49 gives 99.

activities.prompt: Meena has 6 marbles and finds 8 marbles. How many marbles does she have now?

lessons.title: Solving Equations Systematically

activities.prompt: How can you turn a tricky equation into one simple step?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Solving Step by Step
activities.body: Solving equations means keeping both sides balanced. For 5x – 4 = 7, add 4 to both sides. This gives 5x = 11. For 11y + (–5) = 61, subtract (–5) from both sides. Bring unknown terms together. Then divide both sides by a factor. Finally, check the solution every time.
keyPoints: Add 4 to both sides of 5x – 4 = 7.
Remove added or subtracted terms using additive inverses.
Divide by a factor and check the solution.
activities.explanation: Follow each step carefully and check your final solution.

activities.title: Balance the scale

tasks.then: The left side is too light: 7 is less than 11.

tasks.say: Find the x that balances it.
tasks.then: 2 x 4 + 3 = 11, so both sides are equal.

activities.takeaway: An equation is a balance: both sides must be equal.
activities.explanation: An equation is a balance: both sides must be equal.

activities.prompt: Adding 4 to both sides of 5x – 4 = 7 gives 5x = 11.
activities.explanation: Yes. Adding 4 cancels the –4 and gives 5x = 11.

activities.prompt: Which action should you take first in 5x – 4 = 7?
activities.explanation: Add 4 to both sides so the –4 disappears.

activities.prompt: After adding 4 to both sides, the equation becomes 5x = ______.
activities.explanation: The new equation is 5x = 11.

activities.prompt: Match each equation step with its next action.
activities.explanation: Each action moves the equation towards its solution.

activities.title: Removing Terms and Factors
activities.body: When an added or subtracted term is removed, use its additive inverse on the other side. When a factor is removed, divide the other side by that factor. Subtracting 4y from both sides brings unknown terms together. After solving, always check the solution.
keyPoints: Use an additive inverse to remove a term.
Subtract unknown terms to bring them together.
Divide by a factor and check the solution.
activities.explanation: These rules guide each systematic step.

activities.prompt: Put these steps for 5x – 4 = 7 in order.

activities.prompt: What happens with “4 more than a number equals 5 more than a number”?

activities.prompt: A bus depot has 2 equal groups of x buses. After 14 buses leave, 10 buses remain. Find x.
activities.explanation: Add 14 to both sides to get ax=c+b. Divide by 2 to get x=(c+b)/a.

lessons.title: A History of Algebra

activities.prompt: How did ancient mathematicians turn hidden answers into powerful equations?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: An Old Name for Algebra
activities.body: Algebra has an old Indian name: Bījagaṇita. The word bīja means seed. An unknown is like a hidden answer. Brahmagupta explained work on unknown numbers in his book from 628 CE. Indian mathematical ideas were translated into Arabic in the 8th century. These ideas influenced Al-Khwarizmi. His book title means calculation by restoring and balancing. The word al-jabr later gave us algebra.
keyPoints: Bījagaṇita is another name for algebra.
The word bīja means seed.
An unknown is like a hidden answer.
activities.explanation: These ideas helped shape the history of algebra.

activities.title: From India to Arabic
activities.body: Brahmagupta's book was one of the earliest known works on algebra. It explained work on unknown numbers in 628 CE. Indian mathematical ideas were translated into Arabic in the 8th century. They influenced Al-Khwarizmi. His book's title means calculation by restoring and balancing. The word al-jabr later gave us the word algebra.
keyPoints: Brahmagupta explained unknown numbers in 628 CE.
Indian ideas were translated into Arabic.
Al-jabr later gave us algebra.
activities.explanation: Indian ideas travelled and influenced the history of algebra.

activities.title: Seed or Hidden Answer?
activities.prompt: The word bīja means a hidden answer.
activities.explanation: The word bīja means seed. An unknown is like a hidden answer.

activities.prompt: Bījaganita is another name for algebra, and an unknown is like a hidden answer. If 15 laddoos include 3 known laddoos, how many laddoos are the hidden unknown?

activities.prompt: Brahmagupta explained his work on unknown numbers in 628 CE in one of the earliest known works on algebra. How many years old was the book in 900 CE?
activities.explanation: The book's age is year - 628 = 900 - 628 years.

activities.prompt: Indian mathematical ideas were translated into Arabic in the 8th century and influenced Al-Khwarizmi. On a timeline from 701 CE to 799 CE, how many years passed?
activities.explanation: The time from 701 CE to 799 CE is 799 - 701 years.

activities.title: Order the Algebra Story
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order described by the lesson.
items: Brahmagupta explained work on unknown numbers in 628 CE
Indian ideas were translated into Arabic in the 8th century
The word al-jabr later gave us the word algebra
activities.explanation: The first event came in 628 CE. Translation came in the 8th century. Influence and the later word followed.

activities.prompt: In ancient notation, a known quantity was written in rūpa form. A rūpa quantity of 8 marbles is combined with an unknown number of marbles to make 25. How many marbles are unknown?
activities.explanation: The unknown number is total - known = 25 - 8 marbles.

activities.prompt: Aryabhata and Brahmagupta developed systematic methods for single unknowns. A shop has 2 packets, each with x laddoos, and 41 extra laddoos. There are 81 laddoos in all. How many laddoos are in each packet?
activities.explanation: First find the laddoos in the packets with 81 - 41, then divide by 2. The formula is (81 - 41) / 2.

activities.prompt: Jasmine wants an arrangement made with exactly 99 sticks. Which position uses 99 sticks?
activities.explanation: The lesson gives n = 49 as the solution for 99 sticks.

activities.prompt: Trying n = 49 gives a left-hand value of 99.
activities.explanation: Trying n = 49 gives 99 on the left-hand side.

activities.prompt: The solution of 2n + 1 = 99 is n = ______.
activities.hint: Try the value that gives 99 on the left.
activities.explanation: This value makes the left-hand side equal to 99.

Checking different values in an equation

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to solve 11y + (–5) = 61.
activities.explanation: Removing (–5) gives 11y = 66. Dividing both sides by 11 gives y = 6.

activities.prompt: Which equation shows when Jahnavi’s and Sunita’s savings are equal?
activities.explanation: Their savings are equal when the two expressions match.

activities.prompt: Performing different operations on the two sides keeps their equality.
activities.explanation: Use the same operation on both sides to keep their equality.
